guide.title: About GIF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

GIF is an indexed-color raster format that supports both individual pictures and timed image sequences. Every picture in a GIF draws from a palette limited to 256 entries, and transparency works by flagging one entry as clear, so soft edges cannot keep partial opacity. That suits flat logos and badges better than photographs.

For an icon, the real question is which frame carries the drawing.

### Programs that open GIF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP can export a single picture or a multilayer animation as GIF, and ImageMagick reads GIF, though your install's own format list is the final word on support.
- **Web:** Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox display GIF files in the page.
- **Mobile:** Safari shows GIF files, as does Chrome on a phone.

### GIF and ICO compared

- **Names and media types**: .gif and .ico; the registered media type for ICO is image/vnd.microsoft.icon.
- **Content**: a GIF is a palette-based sequence of frames. ICO files may include several pictures and are little-endian.
- **Typical use**: ICO is Microsoft's format for interface icons, and it is widely associated with website favicons.

The page decodes the GIF to pixels and keeps its first frame; delays and looping are not carried over. An image taller or wider than 256 px is shrunk to fit a 256 by 256 square with its shape unchanged, a smaller one stays as it is, and a full-size image goes into the ICO as PNG data. Metadata is dropped.

### Other ways to convert GIF to ICO

- **Pillow:** `Image.open("reaction.gif").save("reaction.ico", sizes=[(16,16),(32,32),(48,48)])` writes several sizes from one frame. The GIF loader supports seek() and tell(), so you can move to another frame before saving.

### Problems with GIF files

GIMP caps GIF exports at a 256-color palette, and gradients may shift as a result; the banding shows up once the picture is small. Look at the result on both light and dark backgrounds at its real size.

High-DPI screens show a small icon blurry, so prepare the largest clean still you have.

Because the output holds one image, prepare the version you want as a still first. A small logo or badge converts best; an animated reaction rarely makes a readable icon.

guide.title: About HEIC files
guide.markdown:
### What is a HEIC file?

A HEIC file is a photo stored in HEIF, the High Efficiency Image File Format, with its pictures compressed by HEVC, the H.265 video codec. HEIF is a container standard from MPEG, ISO/IEC 23008-12, first published in 2017. Apple made it the iPhone's photo format with iOS 11 and macOS High Sierra, and the iPhone 7 and later capture in it. Apple's reason was size: HEIF compresses photos better than JPEG.

One HEIF file can hold more than one picture. It may carry several images or an image sequence, a depth map, an alpha plane stored as an extra image, more than 8 bits per color channel, and Exif or XMP metadata.

Most HEIC files come from an iPhone or iPad: shared to another device, attached to a message, or copied to a computer. A Live Photo is a HEIC still paired with a short MOV video, so its HEIC file holds only the still picture. Some Android phones can save HEIF too, from Android 10 where the hardware supports it.

### Programs that open HEIC files

**Windows**

- Photos: opens HEIC after you add two Microsoft Store apps, the free HEIF Image Extension and the paid HEVC Video Extensions.
- Adobe Photoshop: reads HEIC on Windows only once both of those codecs are installed.

**Mac**

- Photos and Preview: open HEIC from macOS High Sierra 10.13, and both export JPEG copies.
- Adobe Photoshop: opens HEIC on macOS 10.13 or later.

**Linux**

- GIMP: imports HEIC when built with libheif, the open-source decoder this page also runs.
- ImageMagick: converts HEIC on the command line when compiled with libheif.

**Web**

- Safari: displays HEIC images from version 17.
- This page: decodes HEIC with libheif inside the page, so it works in Chrome, Edge and Firefox as well.

**Mobile**

- iPhone and iPad: Photos and Files open HEIC without any setup.
- Android: decodes HEIF from Android 9.

### HEIC and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .heic or .heif, with image/heic and image/heif; .jpg or .jpeg, with image/jpeg.
- **Compression**: HEIC codes each picture as an HEVC still frame. JPEG uses the older 8x8 discrete cosine transform.
- **What one file holds**: a HEIF can bundle several images, depth data and an alpha plane. A JPG holds one picture.
- **Color depth**: HEIF allows more than 8 bits per channel; JPEG stores 8. This page decodes to 8-bit RGB.
- **Transparency**: a JPG has no alpha channel at all.
- **Metadata**: both carry Exif. The JPG made here doesn't get the HEIC's Exif or ICC profile.
- **Where it opens**: JPG opens almost anywhere. HEIC needs the support listed above.

The trade is reach for size. The JPG opens on any device and uploads to any site. It is lossy at quality 0.85, often larger than the HEIC, and carries none of the date, camera or location tags. A burst or multi-image HEIC gives only its primary picture.

### Other ways to convert HEIC to JPG

- **Finder (Mac)**: Control-click the photo, choose Quick Actions > Convert Image, then pick JPEG and a size. On some macOS versions the command sits under Quick Actions > More.
- **Preview (Mac)**: open the photo, choose File > Export, set Format to JPEG and click Save.
- **Photos (Mac)**: select the photos, choose File > Export > Export Photos, and set Photo Kind to JPEG.
- **Preview (iPhone, iOS 26)**: open the file, tap the actions button beside its name, tap Export, then choose JPEG.
- **iPhone camera setting**: Settings > Camera > Formats > Most Compatible makes new photos JPEG. Photos you already took stay HEIC.

### Problems with HEIC files

- **Windows says it can't open the file**: add the HEIF Image Extension and the HEVC Video Extensions, or skip them and convert here.
- **A website won't accept it**: many upload forms want JPG or PNG. Convert first, or use the [HEIC to PNG converter](/heic-to-png/) for a lossless copy.
- **"No images in HEIF"**: the file has no picture to decode. Copy the photo off the phone again and retry.
- **HEIC on one computer, JPG on another**: an iPhone may turn photos into JPEG when they're copied over USB. Choose Keep Originals in the iPhone's Photos settings to get the HEIC files.
- **A whole album to convert**: choose all the photos at once. Each JPG downloads as soon as it's ready.

guide.title: About HEVC files
guide.markdown:
### What is a HEVC file?

The letters HEVC expand to High Efficiency Video Coding, a codec also named H.265 or MPEG-H Part 2. The two standards bodies ISO/IEC and ITU-T wrote it jointly, and its first edition appeared in 2013. The Library of Congress describes it as covering storage, television, streaming and video calls.

A file ending in .hevc is usually the bare coded stream and nothing around it. FFmpeg lists a raw HEVC stream as an input it can read, separate from a wrapper such as MP4. Without a wrapper there is no sound track, only pictures in order.

HEVC defines profiles, and each profile switches on a different set of coding features. The family also reaches higher bit depths and full-resolution chroma. Apple's support began in iOS 11 and macOS High Sierra 10.13, so older devices cannot be expected to decode it.

It is used for 4K and HDR video, for iPhone and camera recordings, and for streaming. It supports 8K and HDR, and patent licensing is required to use it. IANA's registration also says decoders have to handle the profile and level of a stream.

### Programs that open HEVC files

**Windows, Mac and Linux:**

- FFmpeg reads raw HEVC streams on the command line.
- FFplay, the player built on the same libraries, plays them.

**Mobile:**

- VLC for Android: VideoLAN documents HEVC hardware decoding through Android MediaCodec.

### HEVC and MOV compared

- **What each one is**: HEVC names a way of coding pictures, while MOV is a container. MOV is the QuickTime container: Apple shipped MOV in 1991, and Windows users got it in 1994.
- **Extensions**: a QuickTime file ends in .mov or .qt. The video/quicktime media type belongs to it, and video/H265 only describes HEVC sent over RTP.
- **Structure**: a MOV is built from atoms, and software can skip those it does not recognize. A raw stream has no such structure. A MOV is a multi-track container, and besides video and audio it can carry text, timecode and metadata tracks.
- **Contents**: typical MOV contents are pictures coded as H.264, ProRes or Motion JPEG, paired with AAC or PCM sound, so a MOV never promises HEVC inside.
- **Use**: MOV is common for video editing on macOS and for iPhone recordings, while a bare .hevc needs a program that reads raw streams, such as FFmpeg.

This page decodes the stream and writes a fresh file. The picture goes through the x264 encoder (constant rate factor 32, ultrafast preset, zero-latency tuning), and the MOV is written with its index at the front. There is no audio option, since the source has none. Frames marked interlaced are deinterlaced. A picture longer than 1920 pixels on either side shrinks to fit, widths and heights are made even, and playback never exceeds 30 frames per second.

You can pick several files. They run in order, and every MOV is saved separately. Nothing is sent to a server, and no size limit is applied by the page. A long stream takes as long as your device needs.

### Other ways to convert HEVC to MOV

- **FFmpeg, re-encode:** run `ffmpeg -i stream.hevc -c:v libx264 -an picture.mov`. This is the same idea as the page with your own settings.
- **FFmpeg, keep HEVC:** enter `ffmpeg -i stream.hevc -c:v copy -an retained.mov`. The documentation describes `-c copy` as stream copy with no decoding or encoding, so the pictures stay HEVC.
- **FFmpeg with a fixed frame rate:** put `-r 24` before the input, as in `ffmpeg -r 24 -i stream.hevc -c:v libx264 fixed.mov`. As an input option it makes FFmpeg ignore stored timestamps and assume that constant rate.

### Problems with HEVC files

- **A decoder lacks the profile**: supporting H.265 alone does not cover every profile and level, so one program may play a stream that another refuses.
- **Older Apple devices stall**: they can be limited by the resolution or the frame rate of the video.
- **No sound, or an editor will not import it**: a raw stream is not an audio and video container. Use a suitable wrapper when an app requires one, and add audio separately.
- **The page reports an exit code**: FFmpeg stopped with an error. Check whether ffplay can play the same file.

guide.title: Understanding HTML for SVG output
guide.markdown:
### What is an HTML file?

HTML, short for HyperText Markup Language, describes web pages and web applications. The early versions came out of CERN and, later, the IETF (1990 to 1995). Today the WHATWG keeps HTML as a Living Standard. An HTML file says what each part of a page is: a heading, a paragraph, a link, a picture. Appearance comes from CSS, and JavaScript adds behavior.

An HTML file can link to separate files instead of holding every asset itself, so a saved page may depend on pictures, fonts, stylesheets and scripts that stay on the website. Its registered media type is text/html.

### Programs that open HTML files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Firefox renders a local HTML file; open one with Ctrl+O or Command+O.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Visual Studio Code is an editor with syntax highlighting, completion and formatting for HTML.

A text editor shows the markup itself, which is what you check when a picture or style link looks wrong. A browser shows the finished page, which is what this converter draws.

### HTML and SVG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .html goes with text/html; .svg goes with image/svg+xml, and gzip-compressing an SVG gives .svgz.
- **What they hold**: HTML describes a document that a browser lays out. SVG is an XML language that describes two-dimensional graphics as shapes, text and embedded images.
- **Readable as text**: an SVG is plain text, which any editor opens and ordinary tools can search, index or compress. In the SVG this page makes, the words are pixels, not text.
- **Standards**: HTML is a WHATWG Living Standard. SVG is a W3C standard: version 1.0 reached Recommendation status in 2001, and 1.1 followed in 2003.
- **Scripting and style**: both work with CSS and JavaScript, and an SVG can be styled, scripted and animated. This converter's SVG has nothing to animate.
- **Where they show**: major browsers render SVG as a page of its own or inline within HTML.

This converter doesn't turn HTML into drawing shapes. It parses the file without running it, lays the page out 1280 px wide, and draws it to a picture. The picture is wrapped in an SVG as one embedded PNG at the page's pixel size. Height follows the page, up to 4096 px, where a longer page is cut off. The `vh` unit uses an 800 px window. The HTML stays as it was; the download is a fresh file with the same name, for example report.svg.

Scripts, frames, objects, event attributes, `<base>`, `<link>` and `<meta http-equiv>` elements and audio are removed, and nothing is fetched from any site. A video shows only its poster frame, if the file defines one. Inline styles and `<style>` blocks apply. Pictures and fonts apply only when they're included in the file as data: URLs.

- **Inkscape:** take a full-page screenshot of the page, then choose File > Import in Inkscape and pick it. A dialog asks whether to link or embed the image; embedding stores it inside the SVG file, and linking breaks if the screenshot moves. The SVG still holds a picture.
- **modern-screenshot:** the library behind this page lists `domToSvg` among its functions. It runs inside a web page you control.
- **XMLSerializer:** when the HTML already contains an inline `<svg>`, `new XMLSerializer().serializeToString(document.querySelector('svg'))` returns its markup as a string. It extracts existing artwork only; it doesn't convert the rest of the page.

### Problems with HTML files

- **Pictures or styling are missing**: a saved page links to files that stayed online, and without them it loses its pictures and styling. Save the page with its files, or embed them in the HTML, and convert again.
- **The text looks garbled**: the character encoding is wrong or undeclared. HTML defines encoding declarations, so declare it in the file.
- **The SVG ends early**: your page is taller than the converter's height limit. Break the HTML into shorter parts and convert each.
- **The page looks different here**: linked fonts and stylesheets aren't loaded. Put the CSS inline and put the fonts in the file.
- **An editor shows no errors in linked files**: Visual Studio Code limits its built-in HTML analysis to the current file, so it doesn't inspect linked scripts and styles.

guide.markdown:
### What is an ICNS file?

ICNS packages application icon artwork for macOS. An icon collection can supply standard and high-resolution representations. Apple's documentation pairs standard and Retina icons from 16 up to 512 points, and the 512-point Retina image is 1024 pixels wide. Apple's iconutil converts an iconset directory into an ICNS file.

ICO is Microsoft's image format for graphical interface icons. A file may contain more than one image, and Windows Vista icon guidance includes 256 by 256 images for high-DPI displays.

### Programs that open ICNS files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP opens ICNS icons via its Apple Icon Image plug-in, and XnView MP lists ICNS as supported.
- **Mac:** iconutil unpacks an ICNS into an iconset of PNG images.

### ICNS and ICO compared

- **Source image**: the page picks the largest PNG icon in the ICNS.
- **Output**: one ICO image, not a set of sizes.
- **Size**: anything above 256 px on a side is shrunk into a 256 by 256 box, proportions kept. Smaller images keep their size.
- **Storage**: at 256 px the ICO entry is PNG data.
- **Refused**: an ICNS whose icons are all older JPEG 2000 or bitmap types.
- **Several files**: choose many ICNS files at once; each becomes its own ICO, with no ZIP.
- **Privacy**: the ICNS stays on your device, because the page runs in your browser.
- **Metadata**: dropped, since the icon goes through raw pixels at 8 bits per channel.

### Other ways to convert ICNS to ICO

- **Pillow:** open the ICNS, optionally set the `size` property before loading, then save an ICO with a `sizes` list. Sizes above 256 are ignored.
- **GIMP:** open the ICNS, then File > Export As, saving as .ico. Pick sizes and Compressed (PNG) in the icon dialog; GIMP warns that not all programs read compressed icons.

### Problems with ICNS files

- **A small icon looks soft when enlarged**: a single enlarged icon may look different from artwork drawn for the display size.
- **Missing representations**: the system must choose among the sizes that exist.
- **A multi-size ICO is needed**: build each size in a desktop tool, since this page writes one image.
- **Pixel sizes must match iconset names**: iconutil needs matching dimensions before it builds the resource.

guide.title: About ICO files
guide.markdown:
### What is an ICO file?

ICO is Microsoft's image format for the pictures that stand for programs, files and folders in a graphical interface. The IANA registration names it image/vnd.microsoft.icon. One file can hold several images, and its multi-byte values use little-endian ordering.

The most visible use today is the website favicon. The .ico extension is widely associated with the small picture a browser shows in a tab. Desktop icons use the same format for the program images in Windows.

Because an icon is shown at many sizes, one file can carry a set of images of different sizes and color depths. Each entry can be a bitmap or a PNG, and the format supports alpha transparency. Windows Vista guidance from Microsoft calls for 256-by-256 images aimed at high-DPI displays.

Icons are used for Windows application icons and for website favicons. Open them with Windows File Explorer, GIMP, IrfanView or a web browser.

A preview may show only one image, and the file may contain more. If you only need a regular picture, such as a logo for a document, a conversion pulls a flat image out of the container.

### Programs that open ICO files

**Windows, Mac and Linux:**

- ImageMagick reads ICO.
- XnView MP counts ICO among its supported formats; using it at a company requires a license.

**Web:**

- Mozilla Firefox displays ICO pictures in page content.
- Google Chrome supports ICO according to Mozilla's browser compatibility table.

### ICO and JPG compared

- **Purpose**: ICO packages interface pictures, while JPG is a photograph format defined by the Joint Photographic Experts Group. Work on JPEG began in 1986, and ITU-T T.81 appeared in 1992.
- **Number of images**: an ICO holds several. A JPG holds exactly one.
- **Compression**: baseline JPEG is lossy, working on 8x8 pixel blocks with a discrete cosine transform.
- **Transparency**: JPEG stores 8 bits per color channel and no alpha channel, so an icon with see-through corners cannot stay see-through as a JPG.
- **Use**: Photographs online, camera output and email attachments are the usual jobs for JPG. Every major browser can show it, and most cameras and scanners support it directly.
- **Color depth**: an icon's entries come in different color depths, while JPEG always stores 8 bits per color channel.
- **Quality**: JPEG quality commonly runs from 0 to 100, though the same number does not give identical results in every program.
- **Media type**: image/vnd.microsoft.icon for ICO and image/jpeg for JPG.

The conversion happens inside your browser. The page asks the browser to open the icon, draws it as 8-bit RGBA pixels and then asks it for a JPEG at quality 0.85. No EXIF, ICC profile or XMP data comes along, because only pixels reach the JPEG encoder. If the browser cannot open the file, the page shows "Image decode failed." or a message saying the browser can't open that kind of file.

Files convert one after another, and every JPG downloads separately. The page puts no cap on size.

### Other ways to convert ICO to JPG

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick badge.ico -background white -alpha remove -alpha off badge.jpg`. The -alpha remove setting composites the image over the background color, which is what you want since JPG has no transparency. ImageMagick's documentation gives white as the default background color, so -background matters only when you want a different one.
- **ImageMagick with a higher quality:** run `magick favicon.ico -quality 95 -background white -alpha remove -alpha off favicon.jpg`. ImageMagick's documentation describes -quality as the compression level for JPEG encoders.
- **IrfanView:** load the .ico through File > Open, then File > Save as with JPG selected as the type. IrfanView's table has ICO and JPG as formats it can read and save.

### Problems with ICO files

- **An invalid header**: bad image offsets inside the file can throw a reader off, which is not the same thing as a missing file association.
- **Soft, enlarged icon**: Enlarging a small icon for a high-DPI screen can look soft, Microsoft notes, so put a larger image inside the icon.
- **Only one image previewed**: an ICO may contain several images, so check its variants instead of assuming the first preview is the only one.
- **"Image decode failed."**: the file would not open in the decoder your browser provides for images. Another program may reveal what the file contains.

guide.title: Understanding ICO for SVG output
guide.markdown:
### What is an ICO file?

Microsoft created ICO for the icons you see in a graphical interface. One .ico file can hold more than one image, so a program can pick the size that suits a taskbar, a desktop shortcut or a title bar. The format stores its numbers in little-endian byte order, and its registered media type is image/vnd.microsoft.icon. Microsoft's guidance for Windows Vista icons adds 256-by-256 pictures aimed at high-DPI screens.

You meet ICO files as Windows application icons and as website favicons, and the .ico extension is widely associated with favicons. Each image inside is a bitmap, stored either as a PNG or as a plain bitmap, not a drawing made of shapes. An ICO can carry alpha transparency.

### Programs that open ICO files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads ICO images at the command line.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** XnView MP lists ICO among the image formats it reads. Company use requires a license.
- **Web:** Firefox and Chrome both display ICO pictures in a page.

### ICO and SVG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .ico with image/vnd.microsoft.icon, against .svg with image/svg+xml; a gzip-compressed SVG takes the ending .svgz.
- **Contents**: ICO holds a set of bitmaps of different sizes. SVG describes shapes, text and embedded images in XML.
- **Scaling**: shape-based SVGs stay crisp at every size, while an ICO offers a few fixed pixel sizes.
- **Transparency**: ICO images can have alpha transparency, and the PNG this converter embeds keeps it.
- **Readable as text**: the markup is ordinary text, so a plain editor can open and change it, and search tools or compressors can handle it.
- **Styling**: an SVG works with CSS and JavaScript, so it can be styled, scripted and animated.

What this converter makes is not a drawing of the icon. Your browser decodes the ICO into one picture. The page writes that picture as a PNG and embeds it, in base64, in an SVG with a single `<image>` element. The SVG is sized in the picture's own pixels, width and height alike, and transparent areas stay transparent. Nothing is traced, resized or reduced in color. The ICO is left alone; you get a separate file with the same base name, such as favicon.svg. Several ICO files chosen at once each give their own SVG, one after another, with no ZIP.

SVG can embed bitmaps, and a bitmap keeps its fixed resolution however large the SVG is shown. Metadata isn't copied: EXIF, color profiles and XMP are dropped, and only the pixels are carried over. Current browsers show SVG directly as a document or embedded in a web page.

### Other ways to convert ICO to SVG

- **GIMP:** open the ICO in GIMP, which the format reference lists among the programs that open it, then use File > Export As (Shift+Ctrl+E) and pick SVG. The Export Image as SVG dialog has an Embed raster layers as setting; PNG (always) includes raster layers as PNG images. The SVG holds the picture, as it does here.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick favicon.ico favicon.png`, following the pattern of ImageMagick's own `magick image.jpg image.png` example. Its format table lists ICO as readable. This gives you a PNG to use in other programs.
- **Inkscape Trace Bitmap:** choose File > Import to bring in a PNG made from the icon, pick it with the Selector tool, and run Path > Trace Bitmap. Use Update to refresh the preview and confirm with OK. This makes vector paths, but the manual warns that a 100% faithful vector copy shouldn't be expected, and it suits dark silhouettes on a bright background best. A color trace creates one object per color.

Pick GIMP when you want a picture inside an SVG, as this page makes, and Trace Bitmap when you want shapes.

### Problems with ICO files

- **Soft icon**: a small image stretched for a high-DPI display looks soft. Use an ICO that includes a larger image.
- **Only one size converts**: an ICO can hold many images, so look through its variants rather than trusting the first preview. This page converts one picture and offers no way to choose which.
- **The file won't open**: malformed image offsets can confuse an ICO reader. That is a damaged file, not a missing file association. Get the icon again from its source.

guide.title: About images and PDF
guide.markdown:
### What is an image file?

Image files come in two kinds. Raster formats such as JPEG, PNG, HEIC and WebP store a grid of pixels. Vector formats such as SVG store shapes and redraw them at any size. A PDF is a third thing: it describes pages, and a picture is one thing a page can hold. People turn images into a PDF when a form or an office wants a document, when a stack of receipts or scans should travel as one file, or when pages must print the same way on every machine.

This page reads almost any image a phone, camera or computer makes:

- **Web and everyday formats**: JPEG, PNG, GIF, WebP, BMP, AVIF, ICO and SVG.
- **Apple photos**: HEIC and HEIF.
- **Editing and print formats**: TIFF, PSD, TGA, JPEG XL and JPEG 2000.
- **Camera RAW**: DNG, Canon CR2, CR3 and CRW, Nikon NEF, Sony ARW, Fujifilm RAF, Olympus ORF and Panasonic RW2.

PDF itself comes from Adobe. John Warnock's Camelot project, begun in 1991, had become PDF by 1992, and it has been an ISO standard since 2008.

### Programs that open the PDF you make

The images above open in many programs; what matters next is where the PDF opens.

**Windows**

- Microsoft Edge: Windows' built-in PDF reader, with tools to highlight and draw.
- Adobe Acrobat Reader: Adobe's free reader, which also fills in forms and adds signatures.

**Mac**

- Preview: opens the PDF, rearranges its pages by dragging thumbnails and adds notes.

**Linux**

- Okular and GNOME's Document Viewer: the usual desktop readers.

**Web**

- Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari: show a PDF in a tab with no extra software.

**Mobile**

- iPhone and iPad: the Files and Books apps.
- Android: Google Drive's viewer or the Acrobat Reader app.

### Images and PDF compared

- **Extensions and media types**: each image format has its own, such as .jpg with image/jpeg or .heic with image/heic. A PDF is .pdf with application/pdf.
- **What the file holds**: an image file holds one picture, or the frames of one animation. A PDF holds pages that can mix text, vector shapes and pictures.
- **Compression inside the PDF**: PDF stores pictures with lossless Flate or with JPEG. Here a JPEG keeps its own data. An opaque photo in another photo format (HEIC, AVIF, lossy WebP, JPEG XL, JPEG 2000 or RAW) is stored as a JPEG at quality 92. Everything else, a transparent photo or an SVG included, is stored losslessly as pixels.
- **Transparency**: see-through pixels become a soft mask, so they stay see-through on the page.
- **Page size**: one point per pixel. A 3,000 x 2,000 photo makes a page about 41.7 x 27.8 inches; viewers zoom to fit it on screen.
- **Metadata**: a JPEG's orientation tag turns its page, and its ICC profile is kept. The rest of its Exif, GPS location included, and its XMP are left out.
- **Animation**: an animated GIF or WebP gives its first frame.

### Other ways to put images in a PDF

- **Finder (Mac)**: select the images, Control-click them and choose Quick Actions > Create PDF. Pages follow the order you selected the files in.
- **Preview (Mac)**: open an image, choose File > Export, pick PDF from the Format menu and click Save.
- **Preview (iPhone, iOS 26)**: open the image, tap the actions button next to its name, tap Export and choose PDF.
- **Adobe Acrobat (Windows, Mac)**: choose File > Create > PDF from File, select the image and click Open. Acrobat accepts BMP, JPEG, GIF, TIFF, PNG, PCX, RLE and DIB images.

### Problems with images in a PDF

- **More than 100 images**: one PDF made here stops at 100. Split the set and make two PDFs.
- **Over 250 MB**: the page tells you how many images fit. Remove some, or make two PDFs.
- **An image over 50 megapixels**: the page names the file. Scale it down in an editor first; a 48-megapixel phone photo fits.
- **Pages in the wrong order**: use Move up and Move down before making the PDF. Afterwards, Preview on a Mac can drag pages into place.
- **Pages print huge or tiny**: page sizes follow the pixels, so choose your print dialog's option to fit or scale to the paper.
- **Text in a scan can't be searched**: run text recognition in a PDF editor such as Adobe Acrobat.

guide.title: About JFIF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JFIF file?

JFIF stands for JPEG File Interchange Format. The JPEG standard says how to compress a photo but leaves out details that programs need to swap files reliably, such as the color model and the pixel shape. JFIF fills that gap with a minimal wrapper, which is why most files people call JPEGs are really JFIF files.

The wrapper is small. A JFIF file opens with JPEG's start-of-image marker, followed at once by an APP0 segment labeled JFIF. That segment gives a version number, the resolution in dots per inch or per centimeter, and room for an optional small thumbnail. The compressed picture follows. Eric Hamilton of C-Cube Microsystems wrote the first versions, with 1.02 dating from 1992, and the format was later standardized as ITU-T T.871 and ISO/IEC 10918-5.

JFIF files may end in .jfif, .jfi, .jif, .jpe, .jpeg or .jpg, and all of them are image/jpeg. You see the .jfif ending mostly on Windows, where some PCs save pictures downloaded from a browser that way. The file is fine; the ending is what trips up other apps and upload forms.

### Programs that open JFIF files

**Windows**

- Photos: opens .jfif files as ordinary pictures.
- Paint: opens .jfif pictures for quick edits.
- Browsers: show a .jfif dragged into a tab.

**Mac**

- Preview: opens the file and exports a JPEG copy.
- Adobe Photoshop: opens the file and exports a JPG.

**Linux**

- GIMP: opens the JPEG data inside and exports a .jpg.
- ImageMagick: `magick photo.jfif photo.jpg` writes a re-encoded JPG copy.

**Web**

- Every major browser shows JFIF files, since they are served as image/jpeg.

**Mobile**

- Phone browsers display a .jfif image from a web page like any JPEG.

### JFIF and JPG compared

- **Image data**: the same JPEG compression, with 8x8 blocks, a discrete cosine transform and Huffman coding.
- **Extensions and media type**: .jfif is one of several JFIF endings, next to .jpg and .jpeg. All share image/jpeg.
- **Header**: a JFIF file starts with an APP0 segment. Many camera JPGs carry an Exif segment instead, or as well, with shooting details.
- **Extras**: JFIF can hold a tiny thumbnail and a resolution; Exif adds camera settings, dates and location.
- **Color**: 8 bits per channel and no transparency, in both.
- **What this page does**: decodes the picture, then writes a fresh JPEG at quality 0.85 from its pixels, without the thumbnail, EXIF, ICC profile or XMP.

Renaming is the lossless option: change .jfif to .jpg and every byte stays the same. Convert instead when you want a fresh file or many files at once without renaming each.

### Other ways to convert JFIF to JPG

- **Rename on Windows**: in File Explorer, turn on endings with View > Show > File name extensions in Windows 11, or the File name extensions box on the View tab in Windows 10. Then rename the file and replace .jfif with .jpg.
- **Rename on a Mac**: select the file, open Get Info, and change the ending in Name & Extension. To see endings everywhere, turn on Show all filename extensions in Finder > Settings > Advanced.
- **Preview (Mac)**: open the file, choose File > Export, pick JPEG from the Format pop-up menu and click Save. A JFIF is already JPEG data, so exporting compresses it again.
- **Adobe Photoshop (Windows, Mac)**: open the .jfif, then use File > Export > Export As with JPG as the format and click Export.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux)**: open the .jfif, choose File > Export As, change the ending of the name to .jpg and click Export.

### Problems with JFIF files

- **An upload form says the type isn't allowed**: it checks the ending. Convert the file here or rename it to .jpg.
- **Saved images keep arriving as .jfif**: some Windows PCs choose that ending for JPEG downloads. Rename them after saving, or convert a batch here.
- **An app won't open the file**: it may not know the .jfif ending. Rename it to .jpg and try again.
- **You can't see a .jfif ending at all**: Windows and macOS hide many endings by default. Turn them on as described above, or check the file's type in its properties or Get Info window.
- **You need transparency or lossless edits**: JPEG has neither. Use the [JFIF to PNG converter](/jfif-to-png/).

guide.title: Understanding JIF for PNG output
guide.markdown:
### What is a JIF file?

JIF expands to JPEG Interchange Format. It was the earliest layout in the JPEG standard for holding JPEG-compressed pictures. Later layouts, JFIF and Exif, largely superseded it, and .jif files are rarely seen.

Behind the JPEG name stands a committee, the Joint Photographic Experts Group; its work started in 1986. The core standard was published by ITU-T as T.81 (1992) and by ISO/IEC as 10918-1 (1994). Baseline JPEG discards information. It tiles the image with 8x8-pixel blocks, gives each block a discrete cosine transform, and Huffman coding closes the process. With usual settings a file shrinks to roughly one tenth up to one twentieth of the uncompressed picture. Most digital cameras and scanners write JPEG, and all major browsers can show it. Whether you see .jpg, .jpeg or .jif, the picture format is JPEG, and its registered media type is image/jpeg.

### Programs that open JIF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP imports JPEG for editing.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads JPEG at the command line; its format table lists it as readable and writable.
- **Web:** Chrome and Firefox display JPEG pictures.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Chrome display JPEG pictures.

A progressive mode also exists: a rough picture shows first, then gains detail while the rest loads.

### JIF and PNG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .jif and image/jpeg for JPEG data; .png and image/png.
- **Compression**: JPEG is lossy. PNG is always lossless, using DEFLATE (LZ77 plus Huffman coding).
- **Transparency**: JPEG has no alpha channel. PNG supports an optional alpha channel.
- **Color depth**: PNG samples can be 1 to 16 bits deep, while JPEG uses 8 bits for each color channel.
- **Quality setting**: JPEG encoders accept a quality value, usually from 0 to 100, whose meaning varies by program. PNG has no such setting.
- **Standards**: The aim behind PNG was a GIF alternative free of patents. The W3C issued it as its first Recommendation for an image format in October 1996, and the ISO/IEC 15948:2004 edition came later.
- **Structure**: a PNG file opens with a fixed byte signature, and the rest is a series of chunks: IHDR, then IDAT with the pixels, and finally IEND.
- **Metadata**: this page drops it, so EXIF, color profiles and XMP don't reach the PNG.

Your browser's own image decoder reads the JIF, and the page writes the pixels as a PNG. PNG has no quality setting, and nothing is re-compressed with loss. The picture passes through 8-bit RGBA, which matches the JPEG's 8 bits per channel. The PNG shows what the JPEG shows, flaws included: blocks, ringing around edges and softness are already in the decoded pixels. A photo often grows as a PNG, because lossless storage of a photograph takes more bytes than JPEG. Your JIF isn't changed, and several files are processed one after another, each PNG downloading separately as a new copy named after the original, such as scan.png. The page sets no file-size limit. The PNG makes a good working copy for editing, where saving again would add another round of JPEG loss.

### Other ways to convert JIF to PNG

- **GIMP:** when you open a JPEG, GIMP imports it into its own XCF format as a new project. Next use File > Export As (Shift+Ctrl+E), the command for saving in any format besides XCF, and pick PNG.

### Problems with JIF files

- **The browser says "Image decode failed."**: the file is damaged, cut short, or not an image. Get a fresh copy from the source.
- **A transparent PNG was expected**: JPEG has no alpha channel, so it cannot hold transparency and the PNG is opaque. Cutting out a background takes an editor.
- **The PNG is bigger**: lossless storage of a photograph can take more space than JPEG. Keep the JIF for storage and use the PNG for editing.
- **A photo frame refuses it**: some older frames reject progressive JPEG. Export a JPEG with progressive mode disabled.
- **Quality numbers differ**: a given value can behave differently across programs, so identical settings may still produce different file sizes and picture quality.
- **You need the layers back**: JPEG doesn't preserve an editable layer stack, and this PNG holds a single picture. Keep the editing project file.

guide.title: About JPEG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

JPEG is a lossy raster format from the Joint Photographic Experts Group committee. It suits photographs, and the .jpg and .jpeg endings mean the same thing. It has no alpha transparency and stores a grid of pixels, so camera output, web photographs and email attachments are typical JPEGs.

A JPEG of a logo shows the shapes but holds none of the paths or type that drew them.

### Programs that open JPEG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP opens JPEG files for editing; ImageMagick also reads them, but support depends on how your copy was built.
- **Web:** Browsers such as Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox show JPG images directly.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Chrome show them on a phone.

### JPEG and AI compared

- **Extensions**: .jpg or .jpeg on one side, .ai on the other.
- **Contents**: a JPEG is flat pixels. An AI is Adobe Illustrator's native artwork format, where vector objects and placed pixel pictures can share one document.
- **History**: PostScript underlay AI files until Illustrator 9 reworked the format in 2000. Newer files can also include a PDF rendition alongside the Illustrator data.

The AI written here is a PDF made in your browser, with a PNG copy of your picture placed on a page the size of its pixels. It carries no Illustrator data and nothing is traced, so the picture remains pixels and has no editable paths. The JPEG is not uploaded.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to AI

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick photo.jpg photo.ai`. ImageMagick's format list shows both JPEG and AI as readable and writable.

### Problems with JPEG files

Transparent pixels cannot survive JPEG export, so a logo saved as a JPEG sits on a solid background, and that background goes into the AI file too.

A JPEG keeps no editable layer stack. Retain the project file or the original vector artwork when you have one, because nothing in the JPEG can bring it back.

Two editors given an identical quality number may compress differently, so two JPEGs of one logo can look unlike. If the AI file is for print or packaging, start from the original artwork rather than from a picture that already lost detail.

guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

JPEG, from the Joint Photographic Experts Group, is a lossy format defined in ISO/IEC 10918-1 and designed for photographs. It has adjustable quality and no alpha transparency, and it is supported everywhere. Files ending in .jpg or .jpeg are one and the same format. You find JPEGs as digital camera output, as photographs on the web, and in email attachments and photo sharing.

### Programs that open JPEG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP opens JPEG files for editing, and ImageMagick can read them.
- **Windows:** Windows Photos opens JPEG files.
- **Mac:** Preview on macOS opens them.
- **Web:** Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox display JPG in the browser.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Google Chrome for Android display it as well.

### JPEG and AVIF compared

AVIF comes from the Alliance for Open Media and packs AV1-compressed pictures into a HEIF container; people convert JPEGs to it chasing smaller files for the web. AVIF can be lossy or lossless, handles transparency, HDR and wide color gamut, and goes to 10 and 12 bits. A JPEG source brings none of that. This page decodes the JPEG to 8-bit RGBA pixels and encodes them again, so the AVIF is made from decoded pixels, not a repackaged JPEG. Older browsers may fail to show AVIF, so keep a JPEG fallback. Compare the two files at the size visitors will see before you replace one with the other.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to AVIF

- **avifenc (command line):** run `avifenc -q 80 photo.jpg photo.avif`. The `-q` option sets color quality from 0 to 100, where 100 is lossless.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the JPEG and use File > Export As… to write the AVIF. GIMP supports AVIF import and export from version 2.10.22.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick photo.jpg photo.avif`. ImageMagick lists AVIF as a format it can read and write.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **Transparency is missing**: a JPEG cannot hold transparent pixels, so nothing transparent carries into the AVIF. Choose a format with alpha if you need it.
- **An old photo frame rejects the JPEG**: some older photo frames will not open a progressive JPEG, so re-save it with progressive mode off.
- **Quality numbers do not match between editors**: the same quality setting can compress differently from one editor to the next.
- **Layers are gone**: a JPEG holds one flat picture, so keep your project file if you still need the layers.

guide.title: JPEG and JPG: one format, two endings
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

JPEG is one image format with several file endings. The name comes from the Joint Photographic Experts Group, and the standard was published as ITU-T T.81 in 1992 and ISO/IEC 10918-1 in 1994. Most digital cameras and scanners write it, and it remains the web's usual format for photos.

The endings differ because of history, not format. MS-DOS and early Windows file names allowed three characters after the dot, so .jpg became standard on PCs, while Macs and Unix systems used .jpeg. Both stuck. JFIF, the wrapper most JPEG files use, allows .jpg, .jpeg, .jpe, .jfi, .jfif and .jif, and every one is served as image/jpeg.

JFIF was first written by Eric Hamilton at C-Cube Microsystems, with version 1.02 dated 1992. It was later standardized as ITU-T T.871, approved in May 2011, and as ISO/IEC 10918-5. A JFIF file can carry a small thumbnail of the picture, and camera photos usually carry an Exif block with shooting details as well.

### Programs that open JPEG files

Every image program reads both endings. These matter for this job:

**Windows**

- File Explorer: renames a .jpeg to .jpg once file name extensions are shown.
- Photos: opens either ending the same way.

**Mac**

- Finder: renames the file and asks you to confirm the new ending.
- Preview: exports a fresh JPEG when you want a new file rather than a new name.

**Linux**

- Any file manager: renames the file.
- GIMP and ImageMagick: write a new JPEG when you need one.

**Web**

- Every browser shows both endings.

**Mobile**

- Phone photo apps treat .jpg and .jpeg alike.

### JPEG and JPG compared

- **Format**: identical. The same compression, the same data and the same media type, image/jpeg.
- **Extension**: four letters or three. Programs treat both alike.
- **Compression**: lossy, in 8x8 blocks with a discrete cosine transform and Huffman coding, with an optional progressive mode that loads a coarse picture first.
- **Color**: 8 bits per channel, with no alpha channel and no layers.
- **Metadata**: Exif, the ICC profile and XMP stay when you rename the file and are dropped when you convert it here.
- **What this page changes**: it decodes the image and encodes it again at quality 0.85. You get a new file, not a renamed one.

### Other ways to turn a .jpeg into a .jpg

- **Rename it on Windows**: in File Explorer, turn on View > Show > File name extensions (on Windows 10, the File name extensions box on the View tab), then rename the file.
- **Rename it on a Mac**: select the file, choose File > Get Info, edit Name & Extension, then confirm Use .jpg.
- **Preview (Mac)**: choose File > Export, pick JPEG from the Format pop-up menu and click Save. Re-exporting re-compresses the image.
- **Adobe Photoshop (Windows, Mac)**: choose File > Export > Export As, pick JPG and click Export.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux)**: choose File > Export As, give the file a .jpg name and click Export. Every JPEG save re-compresses the image.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **An upload form wants .jpg**: some forms check only the ending. Rename the file, or convert it here.
- **Downloads arrive as .jfif**: some Windows PCs save web images with a .jfif ending. Rename them to .jpg.
- **The date and location disappeared**: converting drops Exif. Rename instead when you need to keep them.
- **Quality slips after repeated saves**: every encode loses a little, so don't convert the same file again and again.

guide.title: About JPEG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

JPEG takes its name from the Joint Photographic Experts Group, the committee that began work on it in 1986. The standard was published as ITU-T T.81 in 1992 and as ISO/IEC 10918-1 in 1994, and its US patents ran out on 27 October 2006. It was built for photographs, and most digital cameras and scanners still write it.

Most files called JPEG are JFIF files: a small wrapper, first written by Eric Hamilton at C-Cube Microsystems, that lets the compressed picture move between programs and platforms. Camera photos usually add an Exif block with the date, exposure and sometimes the location.

A JPEG becomes a PDF when someone wants a document rather than a picture: a photographed receipt for an expense claim, a signed page, a scan for a school or office portal.

### Programs that open JPEG files

**Windows**

- Photos: views and prints JPEGs. Printing to Microsoft Print to PDF also saves a PDF.
- Paint: crops or resizes a photo before you convert it.

**Mac**

- Preview: opens JPEGs and exports them as PDF.
- Photos: keeps the library your camera and phone photos land in.

**Linux**

- GIMP: edits and re-exports JPEGs.
- Gwenview and GNOME's Image Viewer: quick desktop viewers.

**Web**

- Every major browser displays JPEG, and printing an opened photo from the print dialog can save it as a PDF too.

**Mobile**

- iPhone and iPad: Photos and Files.
- Android: Google Photos and the phone's gallery app.

### JPEG and PDF compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .jpg or .jpeg, sometimes .jpe or .jfif, with image/jpeg; .pdf with application/pdf.
- **Compression**: JPEG discards fine detail in 8x8 blocks, which usually shrinks a photo to between a tenth and a twentieth of its raw size. A PDF can carry JPEG data as it is or store pixels with lossless Flate. This converter does the second: it decodes the photo and embeds it as PNG data. No further detail is lost, but the PDF is usually larger than the JPEG.
- **Color**: JPEG stores 8 bits per channel and has no alpha channel, so there is no transparency to carry.
- **Layout**: a JPEG has pixels but no page. The PDF page takes the photo's size, one point per pixel, with no margin.
- **Text**: a PDF can hold real, searchable text, but one made from a photo holds only the picture.
- **Metadata**: Exif, the ICC profile and XMP stay in the JPEG; the PDF gets none of them.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to PDF

- **Finder (Mac)**: select the photos in the order you want, Control-click them and choose Quick Actions > Create PDF. You get one PDF with a page per photo.
- **Preview (Mac)**: open the JPEG, choose File > Export, pick PDF from the Format pop-up menu and click Save.
- **Preview (iPhone, iOS 26)**: open the photo, tap the actions button next to its name, choose Export and then PDF.
- **Adobe Acrobat (Windows, Mac)**: choose File > Create > PDF from File, select the JPEG and click Open.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **The photo is sideways**: phones often record rotation as an Exif tag instead of turning the pixels, and programs that ignore the tag show the photo sideways. [Image to PDF](/image-to-pdf/) reads that tag and turns the page to match.
- **The PDF is too big to email**: this page stores the photo losslessly. Image to PDF embeds a JPEG's own data instead, so its PDF stays close to the photo's size.
- **A .jfif file**: it's a JPEG with another ending. Rename it to .jpg if a program refuses it.
- **"Image decode failed."**: the JPEG is damaged, for example by a download that didn't finish. Get a fresh copy.
- **Blocky edges or smeared text**: that's JPEG compression in the original, and the PDF shows it as it is. Start from the sharpest copy you have.
- **A scanned page is tilted or has dark edges**: the PDF shows the photo exactly as taken. Crop and straighten it in your photo app first.

A JPEG is a compressed photograph. The Joint Photographic Experts Group defined the format in ISO/IEC 10918-1 for photos, and it trades some detail for small files at an adjustable quality. - **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads JPEG, and GIMP brings it in for retouching.
- **Windows:** Windows Photos shows a JPEG.
- **Mac:** Preview on macOS shows one too.
- **Web:** Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox show JPG pictures inline.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Google Chrome for Android do the same.

### JPEG and PSD compared

A JPEG is a lossy picture with no alpha channel and no layers. PSD is Adobe Photoshop's native, proprietary format. It stores layers, masks, adjustment layers, text and color information so a design can be edited later, in RGB or CMYK mode with 16-bit and 32-bit channels.

A PSD made from a JPEG has only the one picture, so the layers are yours to add. This page decodes the JPEG to pixels and writes them with ImageMagick, so the PSD is no sharper than the JPEG. Keep the JPEG as your original.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to PSD

- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the JPEG, choose File > Export As… and give the file the .psd extension. GIMP does not convert every Photoshop feature exactly; some blending modes have no exact equivalent.
- **Photopea (browser):** load the JPEG through File - Open, then run File - Save as PSD. Photopea converts every file you open into a PSD document.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **No text or layers**: a JPEG keeps no editable layer stack, so retype or rebuild anything that was flattened into the photo, and retain the project file next time.
- **Compression blocks remain**: wrapping the pixels in a PSD cannot undo lossy damage.
- **Nothing is see-through**: JPEG stores no transparency, so a design that needs it should go to a format with alpha.
- **Quality numbers differ**: equal numbers in different programs can give a different look and size.

guide.title: About JPG and HDR
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

A JPG file is a photograph saved with lossy compression. The format was defined by the Joint Photographic Experts Group as ISO/IEC 10918-1 and was designed for photographs. The .jpg and .jpeg extensions are the same format.

You meet JPG files as digital camera output, as photos on the web, and as email attachments and shared pictures. The format has no alpha transparency.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP imports JPEG for editing. ImageMagick reads JPG.
- **Windows:** Windows Photos opens JPG.
- **Mac:** Preview opens JPG.
- **Web and mobile:** Google Chrome shows JPG.
- **Web:** Mozilla Firefox shows JPG.
- **Mobile:** Safari shows JPG.

### JPG and HDR compared

- **Extensions**: a JPG uses .jpg or .jpeg. Radiance HDR uses .hdr or .pic.
- **Pixels**: Radiance HDR stores a red, green and blue byte plus a shared exponent for each pixel, four bytes in all. Compared with ordinary 24-bit RGB, that leaves room for much brighter values.
- **Compression**: JPEG is lossy. Radiance HDR uses run-length encoding.
- **Media type**: the registered type for Radiance HDR is image/vnd.radiance.
- **Metadata**: EXIF, ICC profile and XMP from the JPG are dropped.

Greg Ward created RGBE for the Radiance lighting simulation system, where it stores calculated brightness. It is relevant when a renderer or lighting tool asks for an .hdr image. The converter hands it the 8-bit pixels of your JPG, so the extra range of the format goes unused.

### Other ways to convert JPG to HDR

- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick ordinary_photo.jpg radiance_copy.hdr`. ImageMagick lists HDR, the Radiance RGBE image format, as readable and writable.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** from File > Export As, end the name in .hdr or choose Radiance RGBE as the file type. Confirm the name and the export starts, with no options dialog.

### Problems with JPG files

- **Highlight detail is gone**: a JPG that lost its bright detail can't get it back from a format change. Go back to the original capture if you need that range.
- **Transparency is missing**: JPEG can't hold transparent pixels, so choose a format with alpha instead.
- **A photo frame won't show the file**: older frames can refuse progressive JPEG. Turn progressive mode off and export again.
- **Quality numbers don't match between editors**: a matching number is no promise of matching compression or looks.
- **Layers are gone**: a JPG doesn't keep an editable layer stack, so keep the project file.

guide.title: About JPG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

A JPG is a JPEG image, the lossy photo format standardized by the Joint Photographic Experts Group in the early 1990s. The three-letter .jpg ending comes from MS-DOS and early Windows, which allowed only three characters after the dot. A .jpg and a .jpeg file are the same format.

JPEG splits a picture into 8x8 pixel blocks, converts each block into frequencies with a discrete cosine transform, and rounds away the fine detail the eye is least likely to miss. A quality number, usually 0 to 100, decides how much goes. GIMP starts at 85, and the same number can mean different things in different programs. Every time a JPEG is edited and saved, it is compressed again and loses a little more. A progressive JPEG stores the picture in passes, so a browser can show a coarse version first and sharpen it as the rest arrives.

JPG is everywhere: cameras and scanners write it, and almost every website and app reads it. People turn one into a PNG to edit it without adding more loss, or because a site, template or app asks for PNG.

### Programs that open JPG files

**Windows**

- Photos: the default viewer for JPG, with crop and rotate tools.
- Paint: opens a JPG and saves a copy as PNG.
- Adobe Photoshop: edits JPGs and exports them in other formats.

**Mac**

- Preview: opens a JPG and exports it as PNG.
- Finder: Quick Actions convert a JPG without opening it.

**Linux**

- GIMP: edits a JPG and exports it as PNG.
- ImageMagick: converts JPGs in bulk from the command line.

**Web**

- Every browser displays JPG.

**Mobile**

- Every phone's photo app opens JPG, on iPhone, iPad and Android alike.
- iPhone: the camera saves JPG instead of HEIC when Settings > Camera > Formats is set to Most Compatible.

### JPG and PNG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .jpg or .jpeg with image/jpeg; .png with image/png.
- **Compression**: JPEG is lossy, with a discrete cosine transform and Huffman coding. PNG is lossless DEFLATE: every pixel comes back exactly as stored.
- **Color depth**: JPEG stores 8 bits per channel. PNG allows 1 to 16 bits per sample, in grayscale, indexed or truecolor.
- **Transparency**: PNG has an optional alpha channel. JPEG has none.
- **Animation**: PNG can animate as APNG. JPEG is always a still.
- **Metadata**: JPEG commonly carries Exif and an ICC profile. PNG can hold an ICC profile, and its third edition adds an eXIf chunk for Exif. This converter carries none of it across.
- **Typical use**: JPEG for photos; PNG for screenshots, text and graphics with hard edges.

Converting changes the container, not the picture. The PNG holds exactly the pixels the JPG decodes to: no lost detail returns, no blockiness goes away, and nothing becomes transparent.

### Other ways to convert JPG to PNG

- **Preview (Mac)**: open the JPG, choose File > Export, pick PNG from the Format pop-up menu and click Save.
- **Finder (Mac)**: Control-click the file, choose Quick Actions > Convert Image, then PNG and a size. On some macOS versions it is under Quick Actions > More.
- **Adobe Photoshop (Windows, Mac)**: choose File > Export > Export As, pick PNG and click Export.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux)**: choose File > Export As, give the file a .png name and click Export.
- **Paint (Windows)**: open the JPG and save a copy with PNG as the file type.

### Problems with JPG files

- **Blocky patches or halos around text**: those are compression artifacts, and a PNG keeps them. Start from the original photo or a higher-quality export.
- **You need a transparent background**: converting won't remove the background. Erase it in an editor, then save as PNG.
- **Quality drops after repeated edits**: each JPEG save compresses again. Convert once to PNG, edit the PNG, and export a JPG only at the end.
- **The PNG is too large to send**: that's normal for photos. Share the JPG and keep the PNG for editing.
- **Camera details have gone**: EXIF isn't carried into the PNG, so keep the original if you need the date or location.
- **"Image decode failed."**: your browser couldn't read the JPG, most often because a download or copy was cut short. Fetch the file again.

faqs.question: Does converting JPG to TGA improve quality?
faqs.answer: No. The JPG's compression artifacts are already in the pixels, and TGA keeps them. The conversion adds no new loss, but it can't restore detail either.

faqs.question: Why would a game or video program want a TGA?
faqs.answer: Targa is associated with Truevision video boards, and some game and video workflows still ask for it. If a tool you work with wants TGA files, this converts your JPG to one.

faqs.question: Why is the TGA bigger than my JPG?
faqs.answer: JPG throws away detail to be small, and TGA doesn't discard anything, so a TGA of a photo can be larger than the JPG. The page makes no promise about the size.

faqs.question: Is the EXIF data kept in the TGA?
faqs.answer: No. Only the pixel data survives; EXIF, color profiles and XMP stay behind. Keep the JPG if you need its camera data.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a 24-bit and a 32-bit TGA?
faqs.answer: When a TGA is called 32-bit, that normally counts all bits of one pixel instead of each component; the extra eight bits hold alpha. A JPG has no alpha, so its picture has nothing to put there.

faqs.question: Which programs open a TGA file?
faqs.answer: GIMP's official Targa plug-in loads and exports TGA images. ImageMagick reads and writes Truevision Targa, and Adobe Photoshop opens Targa images.

faqs.question: Does the TGA keep the JPG's pixel size?
faqs.answer: Yes. The page doesn't resize the picture.

faqs.answer: Yes. They are the same format with two spellings, and the page converts both the same way.

guide.title: Understanding JPG for TGA output
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

The Joint Photographic Experts Group gave JPG its name and started the work in 1986. The core standard was released as ITU-T Recommendation T.81 and as ISO/IEC 10918-1, dated 1992 and 1994 respectively. The endings .jpg and .jpeg name the same format, registered as image/jpeg.

Baseline JPEG is lossy. Pictures are split into 8x8 pixel blocks, transformed with a discrete cosine transform and entropy coded using Huffman tables, which typically cuts the size to between a tenth and a twentieth. JPEG keeps 8 bits per color channel and lacks an alpha channel, so there is no transparency or layer support. Digital cameras and scanners commonly produce JPEG, and each major browser shows it. The last US patents covering JPEG ran out on 27 October 2006.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP imports a JPEG for editing and exports at quality 85 by default.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads JPG at the command line.
- **Web:** Firefox and Chrome show JPG pictures in the browser.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Chrome display JPG pictures.

You choose the quality when saving a JPG, normally from 0 to 100, and one number doesn't promise the same look in every program. Progressive JPEGs load as a blurry whole that sharpens as more of the data arrives.

### JPG and TGA compared

- **Extensions**: .jpg or .jpeg for JPG, with the media type image/jpeg; .tga for Targa.
- **Compression**: JPG is lossy. TGA files may be run-length encoded, an optional step that saves space.
- **Transparency**: JPG has none. A 32-bit TGA adds an eight-bit alpha channel to RGB.
- **Color**: a 24-bit RGB TGA stores eight bits in each color component, the same depth as the 8 bits per color channel a JPG stores. TGA also supports indexed-color and grayscale images.
- **Quality setting**: JPG quality is a value, normally 0 to 100, that one program scales differently from another. This page passes no quality setting.
- **Related extensions**: ImageMagick groups ICB, VDA and VST with Truevision Targa, so you may see those endings on files of the same kind.
- **Where each is used**: JPG comes from cameras and scanners. Targa was built for Truevision video boards and survives in video editing and game development.

In this page the browser decodes the JPG, then ImageMagick writes the TGA. The picture passes through 8-bit RGBA and metadata isn't copied, so camera data is not in the TGA. The JPG's blocky artifacts stay too, because they are already in the pixels. Converting to TGA doesn't recompress with loss, and it won't bring back detail. Because a JPG lacks alpha, there is no transparency to carry over.

Choose TGA only when the receiving tool asks for it, since a photo stored this way can take more room. The page doesn't resize the picture or change its color depth beyond the 8 bits per channel it already has. It runs in your browser, and the download is a new file sharing the original's name, such as photo.tga. Pick several JPGs and they are processed in sequence; every TGA downloads separately, with no ZIP.

### Other ways to convert JPG to TGA

- **GIMP:** open the JPG, which GIMP imports as a new project, then use File > Export As (Shift+Ctrl+E) and select TGA. The Export Image as TarGA dialog has a Use RLE compression checkbox: checked, the image is compressed with Run-Length Encoding, and otherwise it is uncompressed. Its Origin choice of Bottom left or Top left sets how the image data is stored and has no visual effect.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick fabric-reference.jpg fabric-texture.tga`, which follows the `magick input output` pattern of ImageMagick's own examples. Its format table lists Truevision Targa as readable and writable.

### Problems with JPG files

- **No transparency after converting**: JPEG can't hold transparent pixels, so the TGA comes out opaque. Mask the picture in an editor that writes alpha and save it as TGA.
- **A photo frame won't show the JPG**: some older frames reject progressive JPEG, which loads a rough image first. Save the JPG again with progressive mode disabled.
- **Quality numbers don't match between programs**: the same number can mean different compression in different editors.
- **Layers can't be recovered**: a JPEG holds no editable layer stack, so keep the original project file.

guide.title: JXL to PNG: format guide
guide.markdown:
### What is a JXL file?

JPEG XL is an image coding system from the JPEG committee, standardized as ISO/IEC 18181. It offers lossy and lossless coding, alpha channels, animation, progressive decoding, and support for HDR, wide gamuts and high bit depth. It can also losslessly recompress an existing JPEG file. A .jxl file may hold just a codestream, or wrap one in a box-based container that also carries Exif, XMP and JUMBF metadata. The registered media type is image/jxl.

People convert JXL to PNG when a program cannot decode JPEG XL.

### Programs that open JXL files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP has had stable JXL import support since version 2.10.32, and ImageMagick reads JXL when it has a JPEG XL delegate.
- **Web:** Safari 17 added JPEG XL, and on iOS 17 and iPadOS 17 it decodes JPEG XL web images, which does not establish a separate photo-library editor.

### JXL and PNG compared

PNG is lossless, supports alpha transparency and stores 8-bit or 16-bit channels. A JXL can also be animated. This page decodes the JXL to one picture at 8 bits per channel, so any extra bit depth is lost. ImageMagick compiled to WebAssembly does the decoding, and the result is a PNG named after your file.

### Other ways to convert JXL to PNG

- **djxl (command line):** run `djxl image.jxl image.png`. The extension of the output file picks the format, and an animation writes one numbered file per frame.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the JXL, then use File > Export As… in GIMP to save it as PNG.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** type `magick image.jxl image.png`. JXL is listed as readable and writable, and it needs a JPEG XL delegate library.

### Problems with JXL files

- **A program rejects the JXL**: its decoder may lack support for the profile or level the file needs.
- **Metadata is missing**: a bare codestream lacks the container boxes that carry extra metadata.
- **Only one frame appears here**: this page reads a single image. Use djxl for each frame of an animation.
- **A large image fails**: pictures over about 537 megapixels do not fit here.

guide.title: About M2TS files
guide.markdown:
### What is an M2TS file?

An .m2ts file carries the video, audio and extra streams used by Blu-ray BDAV discs and AVCHD camcorders. It does not pick one codec. Instead it changes the MPEG-2 transport stream layout so that each source packet has a 188-byte transport packet plus four extra bytes, which makes 192 bytes in all.

Blu-ray allows MPEG-2, AVC and VC-1 video in this wrapper, and the format supports HD video. AVCHD was announced by Sony and Panasonic in 2006. The related MPEG type video/mp2t is shared by plain transport streams, so it does not point to M2TS alone.

An .m2ts file is used on Blu-ray discs and for AVCHD camcorder recordings. On a disc or a camera card it sits beside separate clip-information files, and copying the stream by itself leaves those files and the disc organization behind.

Because the wrapper allows several video codecs, a clip being .m2ts does not tell you what you need to decode it. VLC media player, MPC-HC and Adobe Premiere Pro all open the format, and a camcorder or a disc is where most M2TS files come from.

### Programs that open M2TS files

**Windows, Mac and Linux:**

- Playback of M2TS in FFplay comes from the FFmpeg libraries it is built on, and the tool is free.
- FFmpeg reads MPEG transport streams.

### M2TS and MKV compared

- **Layout**: M2TS is a stream of fixed-size source packets, each a transport packet with four extra bytes. Matroska is built on EBML, a binary structure derived from XML.
- **Registration**: the IANA media type for Matroska video is video/matroska, while video/mp2t, which is shared with plain transport streams, is the nearest type for M2TS.
- **Origin**: Matroska developed from the earlier MCF project, and IANA registers video/matroska for it.
- **Codecs**: M2TS permits MPEG-2, AVC and VC-1 picture streams. Matroska leaves the choice of compression method and level open.
- **Extras**: one Matroska file can combine streams of video, audio and subtitles, and the design also includes chapters and descriptive tags.
- **Typical source**: M2TS comes from camcorders and Blu-ray discs.
- **Wrapper content**: an M2TS file wraps video, audio and additional streams, and a Matroska file can hold the same kinds of stream.

This page does not repackage the stream. FFmpeg decodes the clip in your browser, and the x264 encoder rewrites the picture (CRF 32, ultrafast preset). Audio is written as 96 kbps AAC, and anything flagged as interlaced is deinterlaced. A side beyond 1920 pixels is brought down to fit, odd dimensions become even, and the output never runs faster than 30 frames per second.

To copy the streams without re-encoding, use the methods below.

You can choose several clips at once. They are processed one after another, each result is downloaded as its own file named after the original with the .mkv extension, and no ZIP is made. Your original M2TS files are never modified, and nothing is uploaded, because FFmpeg runs inside the browser as WebAssembly.

A long clip needs time because the work happens in the tab, on your own hardware. The page sets no size or time limit, and an exit-code message means FFmpeg stopped with an error.

### Other ways to convert M2TS to MKV

- **MKVToolNix (mkvmerge):** run `mkvmerge -o archive.mkv recording.m2ts`. The documentation names .m2ts among the transport-stream file types mkvmerge parses, and mkvmerge copies tracks instead of re-encoding them. The same documentation says -o names the file to write.
- **mkvmerge with chosen tracks:** run `mkvmerge --identify recording.m2ts` to list track IDs, then `mkvmerge -o archive.mkv --audio-tracks 1 --no-subtitles recording.m2ts` to copy a chosen audio track and skip subtitles. The documentation says --identify probes the file and reports its type, its tracks and their track IDs, --audio-tracks copies the audio tracks whose IDs you give, and -S or --no-subtitles leaves out subtitle tracks.
- **FFmpeg, copy everything:** run `ffmpeg -i recording.m2ts -map 0 -c copy archive.mkv`. The -map 0 option selects every stream, and -c copy leaves them unchanged. FFmpeg's documentation describes that setting as stream copy, with no decoding or encoding.

### Problems with M2TS files

- **Missing clip information**: copying only the stream omits its clip-information files and disc organization.
- **The extension does not name the decoder**: .m2ts does not tell you which supported video decoder the recording needs.
- **Protected disc content**: Blu-ray content can have AACS protection even though M2TS itself supplies no encryption.

guide.title: About M4A and AAC
guide.markdown:
### What is an M4A file?

An M4A file is MPEG-4 audio with nothing else inside. Apple took up the extension for its unprotected music files. Most carry AAC audio, specified in ISO/IEC 14496-3, while some hold lossless Apple Lossless (ALAC), so the extension doesn't name one codec.

The wrapper can carry metadata tags and cover art, and its media type is audio/mp4. Typical sources are music from iTunes and Apple Music, podcasts and iPhone voice memos. Android plays AAC in .m4a files on every version.

### Programs that open M4A files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Audacity brings in M4A audio after you install its optional FFmpeg library, and leaves out protected files.
- **Web:** Firefox and Chrome play M4A audio directly.
- **Mobile:** VLC for Android and mpv for Android play it.

### M4A and AAC compared

- **Layer**: M4A is a container. AAC is the coding inside it. A .aac file is the stream itself, commonly with ADTS headers.
- **Contents**: an M4A can hold AAC or ALAC and carries tags and cover art. The .aac file this page writes holds the audio stream and nothing else.
- **Profiles**: AAC profiles include LC, HE-AAC and HE-AAC v2.
- **Media type**: audio/aac is registered for ADTS and LATM/LOAS transport.

AAC, Advanced Audio Coding, is a lossy codec standardized through MPEG: Part 7 of MPEG-2 and Part 3 of MPEG-4. It succeeds MP3 and covers sample rates between 8 and 96 kHz. You hear it in streaming audio, music downloads and the soundtracks of MP4 videos and on mobile devices.

### Other ways to convert M4A to AAC

- **FFmpeg re-encode:** in a terminal, `ffmpeg -i library_item.m4a -c:a aac -b:a 192k elementary.aac` writes a new lossy AAC stream.
- **FFmpeg rewrap:** the command `ffmpeg -i library_copy.m4a -c:a copy -f adts extracted.aac` keeps AAC as it is, without re-encoding, and can't turn ALAC into AAC.

### Problems with M4A files

- **Audacity shows no import**: the program asks for its optional FFmpeg library first.
- **DRM-protected files stay closed**: Audacity's FFmpeg route can't import them.
- **Tags get overwritten**: when several recordings go into one Audacity window, the project tags become those of the last file.

faqs.question: Does the AIFF keep album art?
faqs.answer: No picture is written, as any video stream, which includes an attached cover image, is dropped. The audio is converted on its own.

faqs.question: Can I queue several M4A files?
faqs.answer: Yes, in sequence. Each result is a separate AIFF file, and nothing gets zipped.

guide.title: About M4A files
guide.markdown:
### What is an M4A file?

An M4A is MPEG-4 audio on its own, with no picture track. Inside you normally find AAC sound or lossless ALAC, plus tags and artwork. Songs from Apple's music apps, podcasts and iPhone voice memos are common examples. The extension alone does not establish quality, because the same .m4a ending covers both lossy and lossless sound.

### Programs that open M4A files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Audacity imports M4A through its optional FFmpeg library and skips protected files, and FFplay plays the container.
- **Web:** Firefox plays supported media directly, with AAC availability depending on system codecs, while Chrome plays supported MP4 audio and the codec inside still matters.
- **Mobile:** VLC for Android is free and decodes whatever the container holds, and so does the mpv port for Android, which the mpv project links to.

### M4A and AIFF compared

- **Names and media types**: .m4a; .aiff with audio/aiff and audio/x-aiff.
- **Origin**: Apple created AIFF as a relative of the IFF wrapper family from Electronic Arts. Its specification is dated 4 January 1989.
- **Compression**: M4A is usually lossy AAC, or lossless ALAC. AIFF often carries uncompressed linear PCM, and AIFF-C extends the family to compressed audio.

The page decodes the M4A and writes 16-bit big-endian PCM, dropping any video stream. FFmpeg runs inside your browser as WebAssembly, so the audio is not uploaded, and a long recording simply takes longer on a slower device.

### Other ways to convert M4A to AIFF

- **FFmpeg:** run `ffmpeg -i interview.m4a -vn -c:a pcm_s24be interview.aiff` for 24-bit audio. It decodes the same way but keeps more bits per sample, and it cannot restore detail the M4A already lost.

### Problems with M4A files

Audacity cannot read M4A until its optional FFmpeg library is installed, and protected recordings are refused on that route. Opening several recordings in a single Audacity window leaves the project with the last file's tags.

A very large AIFF is expected here. If you need only part of a recording, trim it in an editor before exporting.

Listen for clipping and compare the length of the new AIFF with the original.
