guide.title: About PDF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a PDF file?

PDF, the Portable Document Format, is Adobe's answer to an old office problem: a document should look and print the same whatever program made it and whatever device opens it. It began as John Warnock's Camelot project in 1991, which had become PDF by 1992. Its imaging model comes from PostScript and doesn't depend on the screen or printer. PDF 1.7 became the ISO 32000-1 standard in 2008, and PDF 2.0 became ISO 32000-2 in 2017. Narrower profiles exist for particular jobs: PDF/A for archiving, PDF/X for printing and PDF/UA for accessibility.

PDFs arrive as invoices, statements, forms, manuals, tickets and e-books. A page as a PNG goes where a PDF can't: into a slide, a chat message, a web page or a social post, or in front of someone without a PDF reader.

### Programs that open PDF files

**Windows**

- Microsoft Edge: opens PDFs by default on Windows.
- Adobe Acrobat Reader: Adobe's free reader. The paid Acrobat also exports pages as PNG.

**Mac**

- Preview: reads PDFs and exports pages to image formats, PNG among them.

**Linux**

- Firefox: draws PDFs with PDF.js, the Mozilla library this page uses too.
- Okular: KDE's document viewer.
- GNOME's Document Viewer: the default reader on many GNOME desktops.

**Web**

- Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari: open a PDF in a tab.

**Mobile**

- iPhone and iPad: Files and Books, plus Preview on iOS 26, which exports pages as images.
- Android: Google Drive's PDF viewer or the Acrobat Reader app.

### PDF and PNG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .pdf with application/pdf; .png with image/png.
- **What the file holds**: a PDF holds pages that can mix text, vector graphics, pictures, links, bookmarks, form fields and annotations. A PNG holds one grid of pixels.
- **Resolution**: PDF measures in points, 1/72 of an inch, and redraws its text and vector graphics sharply at any zoom. A PNG has a fixed pixel count, so converting fixes the resolution: here, 144 pixels per inch.
- **Fonts**: a PDF looks the same everywhere only when it embeds its fonts. A PNG has no fonts, only the drawn result.
- **Compression**: pictures inside a PDF use Flate or JPEG. PNG is always lossless DEFLATE, so the drawn page is saved without further loss.
- **Transparency**: PNG supports an alpha channel, but pages from this converter get an opaque white background.
- **Pages**: one PDF, many pages; here one PNG per page, named name_page1, name_page2 and so on.

### Other ways to convert PDF to PNG

- **Adobe Acrobat (Windows, Mac)**: open the PDF, select Convert in the global bar, choose Image format > PNG, select Convert to PNG and save. Each page is saved as its own image.
- **Preview (Mac)**: open the PDF, choose File > Export, pick PNG from the Format pop-up menu and click Save.
- **Preview (iPhone, iOS 26)**: tap the actions button next to the file's name, tap Export and choose PNG. You set the image resolution as you export.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux)**: open the PDF and pick the pages and resolution in the PDF Import dialog, with Open pages as set to Images. Then choose File > Export As, give the file a .png name and click Export. Transparent areas stay transparent unless you check Fill transparent areas with white.

### Problems with PDF files

- **It asks for a password**: a PDF locked with an open password can't be drawn until it's unlocked. Open it in a reader with the password and, if you're allowed, save a copy without one.
- **Fonts look different from the original**: the PDF probably doesn't embed them, so each program substitutes its own. Ask the sender for a PDF with embedded fonts.
- **A poster or drawing comes out small**: pages are capped at about 16.8 megapixels, so a very large page gets less than twice its size. GIMP's import resolution gives more pixels.
- **A scanned PDF looks soft**: each page of a scan is already a picture at the scanner's resolution, and drawing it larger can't add detail it never had.
- **See-through areas came out white**: this page paints every page on white. GIMP keeps transparent areas unless you check Fill transparent areas with white.
- **A long PDF floods your downloads**: every page is its own file, so a 100-page PDF gives 100 PNGs. Delete the pages you don't need afterwards.

guide.title: About PNG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

GIF's patent trouble led to PNG, designed as a free replacement. It was published by the W3C in the autumn of 1996 as that body's first format Recommendation, and it later appeared as RFC 2083 and ISO/IEC 15948:2004. A fixed signature opens each file, then chunks follow, for example IHDR carrying the header, IDAT the pixels and IEND the closing marker. A third edition reached Recommendation status on 24 June 2025, bringing cICP for signaling HDR and an eXIf chunk for Exif data.

DEFLATE compression is used, and it never discards data. Each sample can be indexed, grayscale or truecolor at depths running from 1 up to 16 bits, and optional alpha stores transparency for each pixel. Animated PNG (APNG) is part of the current specification as well; software unable to animate displays the default still frame.

Browsers of every major kind display PNG, and screenshots on macOS default to this format. Registered media types: image/png, plus image/apng for animated files.

### Programs that open PNG files

**Windows, Mac and Linux:**

- Editing a PNG is possible in GIMP, which imports it.
- Reading PNG is also something ImageMagick does, though you should inspect which formats your install supports.

**Web:**

- Chrome shows PNG pictures directly.
- Firefox displays them as well.

**Mobile:**

- Safari renders PNG on a phone or tablet.

### PNG and HDR compared

- **Purpose**: PNG is a general lossless image format. Radiance HDR was created for the Radiance lighting simulation software and is also known as RGBE, a scheme created by Greg Ward.
- **Pixels**: a PNG stores samples per channel. An HDR pixel is four bytes: red, green and blue plus one shared exponent. Brightness values computed during Radiance lighting simulation are what such RGBE images hold.
- **Range**: the shared exponent stretches brightness well past what plain 24-bit RGB can express, which is the point of the format.
- **Compression**: PNG always uses lossless DEFLATE, while HDR files use run-length encoding.
- **Extensions**: an HDR file ends in .hdr or .pic, and its registered media type is image/vnd.radiance.
- **Uses**: HDR serves environment maps for 3D rendering, lighting simulation and HDR image storage. PNG suits screenshots, logos and web graphics.
- **Readers**: Blender, GIMP, Adobe Photoshop and Luminance HDR open HDR files.
- **Animation**: a PNG can animate through APNG, but one HDR file holds one picture.

Your browser's own image decoder opens the PNG, and the pixels pass through 8-bit RGBA before ImageMagick writes the Radiance file. A 16-bit PNG therefore loses its extra depth first. The new file cannot contain brightness the PNG never recorded, so nothing is made brighter than white.

The HDR has no transparency, since the page keeps it only when writing PNG or WebP. Metadata is also lost, as the image travels as raw pixels, leaving EXIF, ICC profiles and XMP behind. When the PNG is animated, frame one is what gets written.

The work runs in a Web Worker, and if the worker fails it is retried on the main thread. No quality setting exists. The page handles files one after another, offers each as its own download, imposes no size limit and uploads nothing.

### Other ways to convert PNG to HDR

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick source.png destination.hdr`. ImageMagick's format table lists both PNG and HDR as readable and writable.
- **ImageMagick, format prefix:** use `magick source.png HDR:destination.hdr`. A format name before the file name tells ImageMagick which format to write.
- **ImageMagick and Radiance ra_ppm:** run `magick source.png intermediate.ppm`, then `ra_ppm -r intermediate.ppm destination.hdr`. The -r option converts a pixmap to a Radiance picture, and -g sets gamma with a default of 2.2.

### Problems with PNG files

- **Compression level**: choosing a lower compression setting cannot cost fidelity, since PNG packing is lossless.
- **Layer offsets**: GIMP and other applications can interpret them differently, so skip its PNG offset option.
- **Missing camera tags**: GIMP treats camera tags and profiles as optional, so enable the metadata controls when you need them.
- **Decode message**: the page shows "Image decode failed." when the browser's decoder cannot open the file.
- **Browser message**: when a browser lacks support for the format, the page suggests a recent release of Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari.
- **Bright areas clipped**: squeezing bright values into the usual eight-bit range may throw away highlight detail.

guide.title: About PNG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

PNG, Portable Network Graphics, is a lossless raster format created as a patent-free successor to GIF. It packs pixels with DEFLATE, the same compression ZIP files use, after a filtering step that predicts each pixel from its neighbors. When the guesses are good, as in flat colors and repeated patterns, the file is small.

PNG is flexible about color. A picture can be indexed, using a palette like a GIF, grayscale or full truecolor, with 1 to 16 bits per sample, and it can add an alpha channel so each pixel has its own level of transparency. The current specification also covers animated PNG, which programs that can't animate show as a still image.

That design explains when PNG is a poor fit. A camera photo is full of fine noise that no filter predicts well, so a lossless PNG of a photo is often several times the size of a JPG that looks the same. That is the usual reason to convert: a photo or a big screenshot saved as PNG, and an email, form or website that wants something lighter, or that accepts JPG only.

You meet PNG files every day. Screenshots on a Mac are PNG files by default, design apps export logos and icons as PNG, and many websites use it for graphics with transparent backgrounds.

### Programs that open PNG files

**Windows**

- Photos: views PNG, including screenshots.
- Paint: opens PNG and saves a copy as JPEG.
- GIMP: free editor that exports PNG to JPG with a quality slider.

**Mac**

- Preview: opens PNG and exports JPEG.
- Finder: Quick Actions convert a PNG without opening any app.

**Linux**

- GIMP: the usual desktop editor.
- ImageMagick: converts PNG files from the terminal, one or many.

**Web**

- Any browser: PNG and its transparency display everywhere.

**Mobile**

- iPhone and iPad: screenshots and saved images open in Photos and Files.
- Android: Google Photos and the gallery app.

### PNG and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .png with image/png; .jpg or .jpeg with image/jpeg.
- **Compression**: PNG is lossless. JPEG splits the picture into 8x8 blocks, describes each block as a mix of frequencies with a discrete cosine transform, and discards fine detail; typical settings make a picture 10 to 20 times smaller than its raw pixels.
- **Transparency**: PNG has full alpha. JPEG has none, so this converter fills transparent areas with a solid color, which your browser's JPEG encoder picks.
- **Color depth**: PNG goes up to 16 bits per sample. JPEG stores 8 bits per channel.
- **Best fit**: PNG for screenshots, text, logos and anything you will edit again. JPG for photos you want to share or upload.
- **Animation**: an animated PNG gives its first frame here.
- **Metadata**: none is carried into the JPG.

What this page writes: a JPEG at quality 0.85, with the same width and height as the PNG. Quality numbers aren't shared between programs, so 0.85 here may not match 85 in GIMP.

### Other ways to convert PNG to JPG

- **Preview (Mac)**: with the PNG open, choose File > Export, set Format to JPEG and click Save. Transparent areas are filled in, since JPEG has no transparency.
- **Finder Quick Actions (Mac)**: Control-click the PNG, choose Quick Actions > Convert Image, then choose JPEG and a size. On some macOS versions the command is under Quick Actions > More.
- **Adobe Photoshop (Windows, Mac)**: with the PNG open, choose File > Export > Export As, set the format to JPG, lower Quality if you want a smaller file, and click Export.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux)**: choose File > Export As, type a name ending in .jpg and click Export. JPEG can't keep transparency.
- **Paint (Windows)**: open the PNG and save a copy, choosing JPEG as the file type.

### Problems with PNG files

- **The transparent background turned solid**: JPG has no transparency. Use the [PNG to WebP converter](/png-to-webp/) for a smaller file that keeps it.
- **Text in a screenshot looks smudged**: JPEG blurs sharp edges. Keep text-heavy images as PNG, or shrink them with the [PNG compressor](/compress-png/).
- **The JPG is bigger than the PNG**: simple graphics with few colors compress better as PNG. Keep the PNG.
- **An animation stopped moving**: JPG holds one picture, so only the first frame is converted.

guide.title: About PNG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

PNG, short for Portable Network Graphics, was designed in the mid-1990s as a patent-free stand-in for GIF, whose LZW compression had started to draw license fees. In October 1996 it became the first format published as a W3C Recommendation, and it was later issued as RFC 2083 and as ISO/IEC 15948:2004. A third edition, a W3C Recommendation since 24 June 2025, brings animated PNG, HDR color and Exif metadata into the standard.

PNG is the screenshot format. macOS saves screenshots as PNG by default, and so does Windows when you press Windows + Print Screen. Logos, charts, diagrams and interface images use it for the same reason: the compression is lossless, so hard edges and small text stay crisp. Design tools such as Figma export PNG, and an iPhone saves its screenshots as PNG too. Putting one in a PDF makes it easy to attach to a report, send to a printer or file with other documents.

### Programs that open PNG files

**Windows**

- Photos: the default viewer for PNG, including screenshots.
- Paint: opens, crops and saves PNG.
- Paint.NET: free editor with layers that reads and writes PNG.

**Mac**

- Preview: opens PNG, marks it up and exports it to PDF.
- Photos: imports PNG files into the photo library.

**Linux**

- GIMP: full editor with PNG export options.
- Krita: painting program that saves PNG with transparency.
- Pinta: a simple, Paint-style editor that opens and saves PNG.

**Web**

- Every major browser shows PNG, transparency included.

**Mobile**

- iPhone and iPad: Photos and Files show PNG screenshots and saved images.
- Android: Google Photos, or the gallery app the phone came with.

### PNG and PDF compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .png with image/png, or image/apng when animated; .pdf with application/pdf.
- **Inside the file**: a PNG starts with a fixed signature followed by chunks: IHDR for the header, IDAT for the pixels, IEND to close. A PDF is a set of objects that describe pages, fonts and images, drawn with an imaging model taken from PostScript.
- **Compression**: PNG always uses lossless DEFLATE. A PDF can store a picture with Flate, the same method, or with JPEG. This converter embeds the PNG losslessly.
- **Color and transparency**: PNG allows grayscale, indexed and truecolor images at 1 to 16 bits per sample, with an optional alpha channel. In the PDF, the alpha becomes a soft mask.
- **Pages**: a PNG has pixels but no page size. The PDF page takes the image's size, one point per pixel.
- **Metadata**: EXIF, ICC profiles and XMP don't come across.

### Other ways to convert PNG to PDF

- **Finder (Mac)**: select several PNG screenshots, Control-click them and choose Quick Actions > Create PDF to get one PDF. The pages follow your selection order.
- **Preview (Mac)**: with the PNG open, choose File > Export, set the format to PDF and click Save.
- **Preview (iPhone, iOS 26)**: tap the actions button beside the file's name, then Export, then PDF.
- **Adobe Acrobat (Windows, Mac)**: choose File > Create > PDF from File, pick the PNG and click Open. PNG is on Acrobat's list of accepted images, with BMP, JPEG, GIF, TIFF, PCX, RLE and DIB.

### Problems with PNG files

- **A photo saved as PNG is huge**: lossless compression suits graphics, not camera photos. The PDF keeps every pixel too, so expect a large file.
- **The PDF shows an unexpected background**: transparent pixels stay transparent, so you see whatever your PDF viewer draws behind the page.
- **An animation turned into one picture**: an animated PNG gives its first frame.
- **A screenshot shows private details**: the PDF keeps every pixel, so crop out names, addresses and notifications before converting.
- **"Image decode failed."**: your browser couldn't read the PNG, usually because the file is damaged. Export it again from the program that made it.
- **A small logo prints blurry**: a 200-pixel-wide logo makes a page under 3 inches wide, and scaling it up to fill the paper enlarges every pixel. Export a larger PNG first.
- **Many PNGs, one PDF wanted**: this page makes one PDF per PNG. [Image to PDF](/image-to-pdf/) combines them, one page each.

guide.title: About PNG to SVG
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

A PNG is a raster image: a grid of pixels, each with its own color. It is lossless, so every pixel comes back exactly as stored, and it can hold an alpha channel for smooth, partly transparent edges. PNG began as a patent-free replacement for GIF, and today it is the usual format for logos, icons, interface art and screenshots; a Mac's screenshots are PNG files unless you change the setting.

The grid is also PNG's limit. A PNG has a fixed number of pixels, so printing it larger, cutting it on a machine or blowing it up for a banner shows soft edges and blocky steps. That is why people go looking for an SVG: a vector file describes shapes instead of pixels and stays sharp at any size.

SVG is a W3C standard, written in XML, that became a Recommendation in 2001 for version 1.0 and in 2003 for 1.1. It can hold paths, shapes and text, and it can also hold ordinary pictures embedded inside it. Those two options are the heart of PNG to SVG, and they give very different files.

### Programs that open PNG files

**Windows**

- Photos and Paint: view and edit PNG.
- Inkscape: opens a PNG for tracing into vector paths.

**Mac**

- Preview: views and exports PNG.
- Adobe Illustrator: places a PNG and traces it with Image Trace.

**Linux**

- GIMP: edits PNG and can save a BMP copy for Potrace.
- Inkscape: the free tracing tool on every desktop system.
- Potrace: a command-line tracer for black-and-white artwork.

**Web**

- Every major browser displays PNG, and Figma imports it into designs.

**Mobile**

- iPhone and iPad: PNG images open in Photos or the Files app.
- Android: Google Photos and the gallery app.

Other tracers exist too, such as CorelDRAW's PowerTRACE and a range of online vectorizers, each with its own settings.

### PNG and SVG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .png with image/png; .svg with image/svg+xml.
- **What is stored**: PNG stores pixels. SVG stores drawing instructions as XML text, and can embed pixel images among them.
- **Scaling**: a PNG has one natural size. An SVG made of paths redraws sharply at any size; an SVG holding an embedded picture does not.
- **Editing**: PNG is edited pixel by pixel in programs like GIMP. Paths in an SVG can be reshaped and recolored in Inkscape, Illustrator or Figma, or even in a text editor.
- **Transparency**: both support it.
- **Use with machines**: cutting plotters, laser cutters and embroidery software follow paths, so they need a traced SVG.

What this page makes is an embedded SVG. It does not trace your picture. The file contains a single image element whose data is your picture as a PNG, written by your browser and stored as base64 text, at the PNG's own pixel width and height. Nothing is resized or reduced to fewer colors, and transparency is kept. The result opens wherever SVG is accepted, but it is still pixels inside, it blurs when enlarged, and it is about a third larger than the PNG data it holds.

A tracing program works the other way. Inkscape's Trace Bitmap, Illustrator's Image Trace and Potrace look for edges and areas of color and redraw them as paths. You get a true vector that scales and cuts cleanly, but it is a redrawing: fine detail, soft shading and photos rarely survive well, and simple, high-contrast artwork such as a logo or a line drawing traces best. If you start from a JPG, the [JPG to SVG converter](/jpg-to-svg/) embeds it the same way.

### Other ways to convert PNG to SVG

- **Inkscape (Windows, Mac, Linux)**: choose File > Import to bring in the PNG, select it, then choose Path > Trace Bitmap (Shift+Alt+B) and pick a mode such as Brightness cutoff. Tracing redraws the image as shapes rather than copying it, and works best on simple, high-contrast art.
- **Adobe Illustrator (Windows, Mac)**: choose File > Place to add the PNG, open Window > Image Trace, pick a preset, then save the result as SVG. The trace replaces the placed image, and a high-resolution picture takes longer to trace.
- **Potrace (command line)**: save a BMP copy of the PNG, then run `potrace -s input.bmp -o output.svg`. Potrace doesn't read PNG, and it traces in black and white at a cutoff set with `-k`, which is 0.5 unless you change it.

### Problems with PNG to SVG

- **The SVG still looks blurry when enlarged**: it holds the original pixels. Trace the PNG if you need clean edges at a larger size.
- **A cutting machine or embroidery program ignores the design**: there are no paths to follow. Trace it in Inkscape or Illustrator first.
- **The SVG is larger than the PNG**: base64 text adds about a third. If file size matters and an SVG isn't required, keep the PNG.
- **A trace has thousands of tiny shapes**: photos and soft shading trace poorly. Simplify the artwork, raise the contrast or reduce the colors before tracing.
- **"Image decode failed."**: the PNG couldn't be read, usually because it is corrupt. Save a fresh copy from its source.

guide.title: About PPM files
guide.markdown:
### What is a PPM file?

PPM is the name of Netpbm's portable color pixel-map format. Each pixel is made of red, green and blue samples, with a maximum sample value that may fall anywhere between 1 and 65535. A normal binary PPM announces itself with P6, while the less common plain-text form uses P3.

Several images can follow one another in a raw PPM without any separator. The usual media type, image/x-portable-pixmap, is conventional and is not registered with IANA.

The design is plain on purpose. A PPM has little metadata and a redundant pixel layout, so files can be large next to images prepared for distribution. That simplicity is also why it appears in scripts and image-processing experiments, and why it is often turned into a JPG before anyone else sees it.

### Programs that open PPM files

**Windows, Mac and Linux:**

- ImageMagick reads and writes PPM color images.
- Provided by Netpbm are the libnetpbm reader and tools for working on PPM files.

### PPM and JPG compared

- **Compression**: PPM stores its samples as they are. Baseline JPEG discards information: the picture is divided into 8x8 pixel blocks, every block is passed through a DCT (a discrete cosine transform) before Huffman coding packs the result.
- **Size**: at everyday JPEG settings the result is a small fraction of the raw size, roughly a tenth to a twentieth.
- **Depth**: a PPM may use sample values up to 65535, whereas JPEG stores 8 bits per color channel.
- **Alpha**: neither format holds transparency, since a PPM is RGB only and JPEG has no alpha channel.
- **Name**: the abbreviation stands for Joint Photographic Experts Group, a body whose effort started in 1986.
- **Standard**: two documents define it, ITU-T T.81 (1992) and ISO/IEC 10918-1 (1994).
- **Progressive mode**: JPEG can show a coarse version of the image first and sharpen it as more data loads.
- **Quality**: the scale generally runs from 0 to 100, GIMP starts at 85, and one number can mean different results between programs.
- **Extensions**: the same format sits behind .jpg and .jpeg, and layers cannot be stored in it.
- **Reach**: JPEG is built into most digital cameras and scanners, and every major browser displays it.
- **Patents**: JPEG's US patents expired on 27 October 2006.
- **Media type**: image/jpeg is registered for JPEG.

ImageMagick, compiled to WebAssembly, decodes the PPM on the main thread of your browser tab and writes a JPG. It reads one image from the file, so a raw PPM holding a sequence of pictures still gives a single JPG. Because the page supplies no quality value and strips nothing explicitly, you cannot pick a JPG quality here. If the picture exceeds about 537 megapixels, conversion fails and a message says it is too large.

Nothing is uploaded and no other size limit applies, so a big file mostly costs time. Files are processed in sequence, every JPG downloads on its own and your PPM stays unchanged.

If you need a particular quality, use one of the commands below on your own computer.

### Other ways to convert PPM to JPG

- **Netpbm:** run `pnmtojpeg -quality=90 image.ppm > image.jpg`. The program reads a Netpbm image and writes JFIF to standard output, and n in -quality runs from 0 (worst) to 100 (best), with a default of 75. Values below about 25 can give images that some interpreters cannot read. For a PPM input the output is in YCbCr format.
- **ImageMagick:** type `magick image.ppm -quality 90 image.jpg`. According to ImageMagick, -quality controls the compression level of JPEG encoders.
- **IrfanView:** load the PPM through File > Open, and under File > Save as pick JPG. IrfanView's format table shows PPM and JPG as readable and savable.

### Problems with PPM files

- **Large files**: the redundant layout and sparse metadata make PPMs big next to compressed images.
- **Eight-bit readers only**: certain readers handle just one eight-bit image. pnmtopnm can normalize awkward input, and pamdepth lowers the depth.
- **Gamma surprises**: files labeled PPM sometimes hold sRGB or linear values rather than the specified transfer function, and pnmgamma can reconcile them.
- **Viewer will not open it**: try GIMP, IrfanView, XnView MP or the Netpbm tools, all of which open PPM.
- **Blocky detail**: the 8x8 block approach of baseline JPEG means hard edges and text can show artifacts.

guide.title: About PPM and PNG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a PPM file?

PPM is Netpbm's portable pixmap, a format for color images. Each pixel has three samples, one each for red, green and blue, and the maximum sample value can be anything from 1 to 65535. The normal binary form starts with the signature P6, and the rarer plain-text form starts with P3. A raw PPM can also contain a sequence of images with no separators between them.

The appeal is simplicity: there is almost no metadata and no compression, so a program can write a PPM in a few lines. The price is size, since the files are large next to compressed pictures. IANA has not registered the conventional media type, image/x-portable-pixmap.

### Programs that open PPM files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads and writes PPM color images. Netpbm supplies the libnetpbm reader and tools for PPM processing.

### PPM and PNG compared

- **Compression**: PPM stores samples as they are. PNG compresses them losslessly with DEFLATE, which combines LZ77 with Huffman coding.
- **Metadata**: PPM carries almost none. PNG is built from chunks, and its third edition allows Exif metadata in an eXIf chunk.
- **Transparency**: a PPM stores no alpha channel, while PNG can add an optional one for per-pixel transparency.
- **Support**: PNG shows up in all major browsers and has no known patents that bear royalties.
- **Depth**: PPM sample values can run up to 65535, which is 16 bits. PNG supports 1 to 16 bits per sample.
- **Origin**: PNG was introduced as a patent-free replacement for GIF in the W3C Recommendation of October 1996. It is also described by RFC 2083 and ISO/IEC 15948:2004.
- **Structure**: PNG files open with a fixed signature, then chunks: IHDR (header), IDAT (pixels) and IEND (the end).
- **Image types**: PNG supports indexed, grayscale and truecolor images, so a PPM's red, green and blue samples fit its truecolor kind.
- **Edition**: the PNG specification's third edition was made a W3C Recommendation on 24 June 2025. Animated PNG is covered, and software unable to animate falls back to the default still image.
- **Everyday use**: macOS saves screenshots as PNG files by default, so PNG is a format most people already handle.
- **Newer features**: HDR support arrives in the third edition through the cICP chunk, and image/png is the registered media type, with image/apng for animated files.
- **Media types**: image/png for PNG; PPM's image/x-portable-pixmap is conventional only.

What this page does is read the PPM with ImageMagick, compiled to WebAssembly and running on your device, and write a PNG. It reads one picture per file and sets no compression or color options of its own. The page rejects a picture beyond roughly 537 megapixels. The sample depth of the output is not something you choose on this page. The download keeps the original's name with a .png ending, and the source file stays untouched.

### Other ways to convert PPM to PNG

- **Netpbm pnmtopng (Windows, Mac, Linux):** run `pnmtopng render.ppm > render.png`. It is the format's own toolset. Netpbm's documentation says it scales the maxval automatically to 255 or 65535, so check technical images.
- **ImageMagick (Windows, Mac, Linux):** run `magick render.ppm delivered.png`. ImageMagick's formats page lists PPM as readable and writable, and PNG as well.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the PPM, then choose File > Export As (Shift+Ctrl+E) and export it as a PNG. GIMP's PNM plug-in loads pnm, ppm, pgm, pbm, pfm and pam files.

The page uses ImageMagick, so the second method is the closest to what it does.

### Problems with PPM files

- **The file is huge**: PPM uses a redundant representation with little image metadata, so files are bulky next to compressed distribution formats.
- **A program reads only some PPM files**: some readers implement only one eight-bit image. Normalize complex input with pnmtopnm and reduce sample depth with pamdepth when necessary.
- **Colors look wrong**: a file labeled PPM now and then holds sRGB or linear values rather than the transfer function the format specifies. pnmgamma can reconcile the variants.
- **Only one picture comes out**: a raw PPM can contain a sequence of images without separators, but the page writes a single PNG per file. Split the sequence first if you need every picture.
- **The sample values run high**: a PPM's maximum sample value may be anywhere from 1 to 65535, so it can hold more than eight bits per sample.

guide.title: About PSD and GIF
guide.markdown:
### What is a PSD file?

Adobe Photoshop saves its working documents as PSD. Inside are the layers, masks, adjustment layers and text that let a designer reopen and keep editing, in RGB or CMYK. Designers lean on it for mockups and retouching, and Adobe owns the specification.

Every file starts with the signature 8BPS, then come blocks for image resources, layer and mask data, and the merged image. Each side can be 30,000 pixels at most; PSB lifts that ceiling. Its registered media type is image/vnd.adobe.photoshop.

### Programs that open PSD files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick can read PSD, and so can GIMP. XnView MP also handles PSD, though business use needs a paid license.
- **Web:** Photopea treats PSD as its home format; choose File > Open to load one.

### PSD and GIF compared

- **Color**: a PSD can store 1, 8, 16 or 32 bits for each channel, while a GIF frame draws from a table capped at 256 colors.
- **Compression**: PSD stores pixels uncompressed or packed with RLE or ZIP, whereas GIF packs them with lossless LZW.
- **Transparency**: a GIF pixel is either see-through or not, with nothing in between.
- **Structure**: a PSD keeps layers and masks, while a GIF may hold many frames, though this page writes only one.

ImageMagick decodes one picture from the PSD and encodes it as GIF. No timed sequence is built from the layers.

### Other ways to convert PSD to GIF

- **GIMP still export:** open the PSD, pick File > Export As, choose GIF and keep As animation unticked. GIMP limits the export to 256 colors, and switching the image to indexed mode beforehand gives the best results.
- **GIMP animation export:** give every frame its own layer, export as GIF, tick As animation, then choose the frame delay and disposal. Layer groups are not supported.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick 'design.psd[0]' preview.gif`. The [0] picks the first image stored in the file, and the quotes stop the shell from reading the brackets.

### Problems with PSD files

- **The file is too big for PSD**: a canvas wider or taller than the 30,000 pixel ceiling has to go into PSB or some other format.
- **Layers and masks vanish on export**: a flattened export can't hold the editable layers and masks, so hold on to the PSD.
- **Another program opens it oddly**: programs other than Photoshop must interpret its private structures, so a working preview doesn't promise that every layer behaves the same.

guide.title: About QT and MP4 files
guide.markdown:
### What is a QT file?

A .qt file is a QuickTime movie. Apple introduced the format in 1991, and a Windows version followed in 1994; it is the same format as ordinary MOV files, which use the .mov ending. The registered media type is video/quicktime. Inside, QuickTime is organized as atoms, and software that meets an unknown atom can skip over it.

Motion JPEG, ProRes and H.264 are all possible for the pictures, with AAC or uncompressed PCM for the sound. That variety is why the ending alone tells you little: a movie can use a codec the destination editor lacks. Screen recordings made on a Mac are written as MOV files. Browsers support MOV only to a limited degree, and Apple now generally uses MP4 itself, so that is the common reason to convert.

### Programs that open QT files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ffplay, the player that ships with FFmpeg, plays QuickTime files through FFmpeg's MOV demuxer from the command line. mpv is a desktop player where you can also choose among the audio and subtitle streams during playback.
- **Windows and Mac:** Adobe Premiere imports this container when the necessary decoder is available.
- **Mobile:** on a phone, VLC for Android is a free player whose decoding follows from what the container holds, and VLC for iOS is an iPhone and iPad player covering most movie formats, from local or network sources.

### QT and MP4 compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .qt or .mov with video/quicktime; .mp4 or .m4v with video/mp4.
- **Lineage**: MPEG-4's file format grew out of QuickTime, but MOV and MP4 are different formats and cannot stand in for each other. The MP4 file format is MPEG-4 Part 14, from 2003.
- **Structure**: MP4 is made of nested boxes, which is QuickTime's idea of atoms under another name.
- **Codecs**: H.264 with AAC is typical in an MP4, and AV1, VP9, MP3 and Opus can live there too.
- **Reach**: every major browser plays MP4, whereas browser support for MOV is limited.

Wrapper and codecs both change. After decoding, FFmpeg encodes H.264 (ultrafast preset, CRF 32) and AAC at 96 kbps, and the MP4's index is placed up front. The picture is shrunk when its longer side tops 1920 pixels, 30 fps is the ceiling for frame rate, and both sides come out even. The deinterlacing filter is applied to frames the file marks as interlaced. Audio is always encoded again as AAC, even if the movie already used it. The page offers no quality or trim controls, and files are converted one after another; every MP4 is its own download and nothing is zipped.

### Other ways to convert QT to MP4

- **FFmpeg, full re-encode (Windows, Mac, Linux):** run `ffmpeg -i legacy.qt -c:a aac -c:v libx264 quicktime-delivery.mp4`. It decodes and encodes again, so the source codecs must first be decodable.
- **FFmpeg, stream copy (Windows, Mac, Linux):** the command is `ffmpeg -i legacy.qt -c copy quicktime-remux.mp4`. It puts the streams into an MP4 untouched, which works only with streams the MP4 muxer can carry.
- **FFmpeg, first seconds only (Windows, Mac, Linux):** run `ffmpeg -t 10 -i legacy.qt -c:v libx264 -c:a aac first-ten.mp4`. The `-t` option, given before `-i`, restricts how much input is read; this page has no trim control of its own.

A stream copy does not re-encode, so it keeps the original codecs. Re-encoding is the choice when the receiving program needs H.264 and AAC.

### Problems with QT files

- **An editor rejects the file**: a QuickTime container can use codecs that the destination editor does not have. Check the codec, because the ending settles nothing.
- **A renamed file fails**: altering the filename ending neither transcodes the video nor supplies the decoder it needs.
- **The file is damaged after an interrupted write**: regular MOV files may be unusable after an interrupted write, and fragmented output has a different recovery behavior. Copy or record the file again.
- **Combing on moving edges**: only frames flagged as interlaced are deinterlaced here, so footage that is interlaced but unflagged keeps its combing.
- **Frame size is smaller than expected**: a source whose longer side exceeds 1920 pixels is shrunk to fit. Keep the QT if you need the full size.

guide.title: Understanding RAF and JPG
guide.markdown:
### What is a RAF file?

RAF is Fujifilm's original camera RAW format. Unprocessed sensor data and a small embedded JPEG preview make up the file, so it is raw material for developing a photo and not a finished picture. Cameras such as the X-T3 can record RAF either uncompressed or losslessly compressed.

Many Fujifilm cameras also offer RAW+JPEG recording, which saves a ready-to-use JPEG next to the RAF. If you shot that way, the JPEG already exists. A RAF is the file to convert when you want to develop the capture yourself, or when you shot RAW only. Fujifilm supplies its own RAW converter for X-series RAF data, and Film Simulation can be applied while the file is developed. The format is proprietary to Fujifilm, and photographers use it for editing before they convert to JPEG.

### Programs that open RAF files

- **Windows and Mac:** RAW FILE CONVERTER EX powered by SILKYPIX is Fujifilm's own RAW development software, so check its camera compatibility list. It develops RAF data recorded by X-series cameras and can apply Film Simulation during development. FUJIFILM X RAW STUDIO uses a connected compatible camera's image processor for the conversion.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick lists RAF as a readable camera RAW format.
- **Linux:** darktable recognizes RAF for import, with camera support from its RawSpeed library.

### RAF and JPG compared

- **Extensions and types**: .raf, and .jpg or .jpeg with image/jpeg.
- **What each is**: a RAF holds the sensor data and a preview. A JPG is a finished picture with the look chosen, in compressed pixels.
- **Compression**: a RAF's lossless option is reversible. JPEG discards data as it compresses: 8x8 pixel blocks go through a discrete cosine transform, and entropy coding comes last.
- **Color**: JPEG stores 8 bits per color channel.
- **Quality numbers**: programs usually offer a 0 to 100 quality scale, yet one number does not mean the same quality everywhere, so a JPG from another tool at the same setting may look different.
- **Loading**: progressive JPEGs exist too, where a coarse version of the image appears first and sharpens as more data loads.
- **Transparency and layers**: JPEG has no alpha channel and cannot store layers, so a JPG carries no editing history.
- **Support**: every major browser displays JPEG, and most digital cameras and scanners write it natively. Its US patents expired on 27 October 2006.

Your RAF is read in your browser by ImageMagick compiled to WebAssembly, which loads the first time you convert. ImageMagick reads camera RAW with its LibRaw decoder and then writes the JPG. The page passes no quality setting and has no development controls such as white balance or Film Simulation. Anything larger than about 537 megapixels is refused as too large to convert here. Your RAF itself stays untouched; what you save is a separate JPG.

### Other ways to convert RAF to JPG

- **FUJIFILM X RAW STUDIO:** on the camera, choose USB RAW CONVERSION under SET UP and connect it to the computer. In the software, pick the source image folder, which must be on the computer's drive, select the RAW files in Thumbnail View, adjust Conversion Settings and click Convert. The output is a JPEG or TIFF, saved in the same folder. The connected camera must be the model that took the photos.
- **darktable:** select the images, open export, choose file on disk as the target, pick JPEG for the format and run the export. Check the camera-support list first.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick photo.raf delivery.jpg`, which reads the RAF and writes the JPG.

### Problems with RAF files

- **The file won't open in an older program**: new camera models can require a converter update, and Fujifilm publishes the models it adds. A losslessly compressed RAF needs software that understands that variant.
- **"The RAW file is damaged"**: the decoder found a broken structure or couldn't decode the picture data. Copy the file from the card again.
- **The RAW data stops short**: the RAF is incomplete, as a copy interrupted part way would be.
- **Size refused**: the file declares a picture above roughly 537 megapixels, or the decoder would need more memory than it may use.
- **X RAW STUDIO won't start**: it requires a supported camera connection and doesn't convert with the computer's processor.

seo.description: Convert RMVB videos to MP4 in your browser. H.264 with AAC sound, scaled down past 1920 px and limited to 30 frames a second. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.question: How do I convert RMVB to MP4?
faqs.answer: Add the RMVB above, let FFmpeg re-encode it locally and download the MP4. A long movie takes time, since your own device does the work.

faqs.question: Can I play an RMVB without converting it?
faqs.answer: Yes, in a player that reads RealMedia. RealPlayer HD lists RMVB playback, and ffplay plays supported RealMedia streams. An MP4 plays on nearly every device, which is the usual reason to convert.

faqs.question: Which codecs end up in the MP4?
faqs.answer: Video is encoded as H.264 and sound as AAC. The settings are fixed: x264's ultrafast preset at CRF 32, and 96 kbps for the audio.

faqs.question: Will the MP4 look better than my RMVB?
faqs.answer: No. The MP4 is encoded from the decoded RMVB, so converting adds no detail. It makes the movie playable in more places, not sharper.

faqs.question: Is my movie resized?
faqs.answer: Only when it is big. A movie whose picture exceeds 1920 pixels on the longer side is scaled down to fit that bound, while smaller ones keep their dimensions. Footage above 30 fps loses frames to reach that rate, with no change to the clip's length. Odd widths or heights lose a single pixel, since the encoder wants even numbers.

faqs.question: Is my RMVB uploaded anywhere?
faqs.answer: No. FFmpeg, built as WebAssembly, runs in your browser tab, so the file never leaves your device. The RMVB itself stays as it was; the MP4 is a new copy named after it.

faqs.question: What does an FFmpeg error mean for my RMVB?
faqs.answer: The message "FFmpeg failed with exit code" means FFmpeg stopped on that file. See whether the file plays in ffplay or RealPlayer HD first. A .ram file points to a stream and holds no video, so there is nothing in it to convert.

faqs.question: Can I convert several RMVB files at once?
faqs.answer: Yes, one after another. Every RMVB produces a separate MP4 and nothing is merged, so a movie that was split into CD1 and CD2 stays in two pieces until you join them in a video editor.

faqs.question: Can I just rename the .rmvb file to .mp4?
faqs.answer: No. Renaming changes only the name, and the data inside stays RealMedia with RealVideo pictures. Converting writes an MP4 with H.264 video.

faqs.question: Is there a size limit for the RMVB?
faqs.answer: The page sets no file-size or time limit. A long file takes as long as your device needs.

guide.title: About RMVB files
guide.markdown:
### What is an RMVB file?

RMVB stands for RealMedia Variable Bitrate. It belongs to the RealMedia family from RealNetworks, and the Library of Congress describes the .rmvb ending as variable-bitrate RealMedia video. RealVideo can be encoded toward an average bitrate or toward a constant visual quality, and the versions differ in efficiency: RealVideo 9 and 10 do not code the picture equally well. A RealMedia file can also carry descriptive information such as a title, an author and a copyright line. Its media type is application/vnd.rn-realmedia.

The format was popular for sharing movies in the early 2000s, so RMVB files turn up in old download collections and archived TV episodes. It is a proprietary RealNetworks format, and today it counts as a legacy one, with the older downloaded movies and media archives as its main remaining use. One thing that looks like an RMVB but is not one is the .ram file. It is a small reference file used in some RealMedia streaming setups, and it points to the video instead of holding it.

### Programs that open RMVB files

**Windows**

- RealPlayer HD: the vendor lists playback of RMVB videos, along with its Windows requirements.

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- FFmpeg: includes a RealMedia demuxer and codec-specific handling.
- ffplay: plays supported RealMedia streams through the FFmpeg libraries.

### RMVB and MP4 compared

- **Names and media types**: .rmvb is application/vnd.rn-realmedia. .mp4 is defined in ISO/IEC 14496-14.
- **Contents**: an RMVB carries RealVideo pictures. MP4 is a wrapper that can hold video made with several codecs, with H.264 and AAC the usual pairing. MP4 turns up in web video, streaming sites and files passed between people.
- **Bitrate**: an RMVB varies its bitrate through the movie. An MP4 holds whatever its encoder produced, constant or variable.
- **Extras**: MP4 can carry metadata alongside the streams.
- **Playback**: nearly every phone, TV and browser plays MP4. Playing one takes a reader for RealMedia and a RealVideo decoder.

The conversion itself: your browser runs FFmpeg, which reads the RealMedia file. Pictures larger than 1920 pixels are scaled down until they fit, anything above 30 frames per second is thinned out, with the running time unchanged, and widths and heights are trimmed to even values. Nothing leaves your device while this runs, and the RMVB itself is never altered. Each finished movie downloads as a new file with your RMVB's name and an .mp4 ending. Then x264 encodes H.264 video with its ultrafast preset at CRF 32, and FFmpeg's AAC encoder writes the sound at 96 kbps. Because the picture is compressed a second time, detail the RMVB had already lost stays lost.

### Other ways to convert RMVB to MP4

- **FFmpeg:** on the command line, `ffmpeg -i archive.rmvb -c:v libx264 -c:a aac archive.mp4` does the job by demuxing the RealMedia file and decoding its RealVideo. Here -i is the input file, and the two -c options pick the encoders for picture and sound. FFmpeg also has a special codec value, copy, that skips re-encoding, but copy would carry the RealVideo pictures over unchanged instead of making H.264, so name encoders as above.
- **VLC:** select Media > Convert/Save, click Add, choose the RMVB and click Open. VLC then shows a Convert window. Type a name for the destination file, pick a profile whose output is MP4 and click Start.

### Problems with RMVB files

- **It won't play on a phone or TV**: an RMVB needs a RealMedia reader and a RealVideo decoder, and many players lack them. Convert the file to MP4 here, or play it in RealPlayer HD.
- **The file is a .ram**: it only points to a stream. Find the actual .rmvb it names.
- **FFmpeg rejects the header**: FFmpeg turns down an invalid RealMedia header instead of guessing. If ffplay cannot open the file either, download it again.
- **A renamed file still fails**: changing .rmvb to .mp4 leaves the RealMedia data inside. Convert the file instead.
- **The download stopped early**: a cut-short or damaged RMVB usually still converts, and the MP4 is then shorter than the movie. Download the whole file again to get the full length.
- **The two halves of a movie are separate files**: converting never joins files. Join the MP4 files in a video editor.

faqs.question: How do I convert an SVG to HTML?
faqs.answer: Choose the SVG above and save the HTML page when it finishes. The drawing is placed inside a new web page, and several files give one page each.

faqs.question: Is the drawing still vector in the HTML page?
faqs.answer: Yes. The `<svg>` markup is copied into the page as it is, so it scales without losing sharpness. Nothing is turned into an image.

faqs.question: Does it rebuild my design as a website?
faqs.answer: No. You get one page with the drawing in it. Shapes aren't converted to paragraphs, buttons or a layout, so a drawing that looks like a web interface is still a drawing.

faqs.question: How is the drawing sized and placed?
faqs.answer: The page has no margins, and the drawing is centered in the window. It shrinks to fit the window's width and is never enlarged by the page.

faqs.question: What is the page title?
faqs.answer: The word image, whatever your SVG was called. The title is set in the page's head, so you can edit it afterward.

faqs.question: My file starts with an XML declaration. Is that a problem?
faqs.answer: No. The XML declaration, doctype and comments before the `<svg>` tag are dropped, because HTML doesn't allow them there. Everything from the `<svg>` tag on is kept.

faqs.question: Why does it say the file has no SVG drawing in it?
faqs.answer: The converter looks for an `<svg>` tag and found none. Open the file in a text editor to check that it is an SVG and not some other XML.

faqs.question: What does the HTML around the drawing contain?
faqs.answer: A doctype, an html tag with lang set to en, a utf-8 charset tag, a viewport tag, a title and one short style block, followed by your svg element.

faqs.question: Do I need to keep the SVG file next to the HTML?
faqs.answer: No. The drawing's markup is copied into the page, so the HTML never reads the SVG file again.

faqs.question: Can I do a whole folder of SVGs in one go?
faqs.answer: Yes. Select several SVGs and each becomes its own HTML page, downloaded separately.

guide.title: Understanding SVG and HTML
guide.markdown:
### What is an SVG file?

The name SVG stands for Scalable Vector Graphics, a W3C standard built on XML. A file lists the shapes, text and embedded pictures that make up a flat drawing. The W3C published version 1.0 as a Recommendation in 2001, and version 1.1 followed in 2003. The shapes are stored as instructions, which lets a renderer draw the same SVG at any size and keep its edges crisp.

Because the file is just text, any text editor opens it, and it can be searched, indexed and compressed; a gzip-compressed one ends in .svgz. Stylesheets and scripts can act on the drawing, which allows styling, scripting and animation, and the format includes clipping paths, masks and filter effects. Its media type is image/svg+xml, and every major browser displays it. On the web SVG typically carries logos, icons, illustrations, diagrams, charts and maps. You can show an SVG on its own or place it inside an HTML page.

### Programs that open SVG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Native SVG editing is what Inkscape does; Mozilla Firefox displays the format, and the list of programs that open it also names Adobe Illustrator and Figma.
- **Mobile:** Google Chrome and Safari display SVG, so a phone browser shows a drawing with no extra app.

### SVG and HTML compared

- **Extensions and types**: .svg with image/svg+xml, and .html with text/html.
- **What each is**: an SVG describes a drawing. HTML is the markup language used to describe web documents and applications, and the WHATWG maintains it as a Living Standard. Its early revisions developed at CERN and then the IETF during 1990 to 1995.
- **Roles**: HTML describes document meaning, CSS supplies presentation and JavaScript can add behavior.
- **Size**: an HTML document may point to other files instead of holding every asset inside itself. Here the drawing sits inside the page, so nothing else is needed.
- **Opening the result**: Firefox displays HTML files from your disk, and Visual Studio Code offers syntax highlighting, completion and formatting for editing them, with built-in analysis that covers only the open file.
- **Encoding**: HTML defines encoding declarations, and an incorrect character encoding can make a document's text render incorrectly. The page made here declares utf-8.
- **Uses**: HTML serves web pages, HTML email, and generated reports and tables.

Your SVG is turned into a web page in your browser. The converter copies the `<svg>` element and everything after it into a new HTML file, and drops the XML declaration, doctype and comments in front of it, which HTML doesn't allow there. The page has a doctype, `lang="en"`, a viewport tag and a title, which reads image. A short style block removes the page margins, centers the drawing in the window and lets it shrink to the window's width. The drawing stays vector. It is not converted to paragraphs, buttons or a rebuilt site layout. A file with no `<svg>` in it is refused with "This file has no SVG drawing in it."

### Other ways to convert SVG to HTML

- **Inline SVG in a text editor:** paste the entire SVG file into the body of an HTML document, as Mozilla documents for SVG in HTML. Keep the viewBox so the drawing scales. Save it with an .html ending and open it in a browser.
- **A CSS background:** give an element a size and set its background-image property to url("logo.svg"). Mozilla lists CSS background-image among the places browsers support SVG images.

### Problems with SVG files

- **A picture is missing**: pictures an SVG references by file name may vanish when those files are unavailable. Preserve the files with the SVG, or embed the pictures in it so the drawing carries everything it shows.
- **The text looks different**: the drawing's text relies on installed fonts, and a stand-in font can change how it looks.
- **An embedded photo looks soft when enlarged**: an SVG may contain pixel images, which keep their own resolution when scaled up; only the vector parts remain crisp.
- **Scripts and links don't work as an image**: an SVG drawn as an image has JavaScript disabled and can't load external resources, apart from data: URLs. A drawing placed inline in a page is not an image in that sense.

guide.title: About SVG files
guide.markdown:
### What is an SVG file?

SVG, Scalable Vector Graphics, is an open standard from the W3C. SVG 1.0 became a Recommendation in 2001 and SVG 1.1 in 2003. An SVG file is XML text that describes a two-dimensional drawing as shapes, paths, text and embedded images. Because it stores drawing instructions rather than pixels, it can be drawn at any size and stay sharp.

Being text has side effects. An SVG can be opened in a text editor, searched, indexed and compressed; a gzip-compressed copy uses the .svgz ending. It works with CSS and JavaScript, so it can be styled, animated and scripted, and it supports clipping paths, masks and filter effects. An SVG can stand alone as a file or sit inside an HTML page.

You meet SVG files as logos, icons, charts and diagrams. Design tools such as Figma, Illustrator and Inkscape export them, icon libraries ship them, and many websites draw their logos with them. The catch is that many apps and upload forms accept only raster images, and some refuse SVG because it can carry scripts.

### Programs that open SVG files

**Windows**

- Inkscape: free vector editor that uses SVG as its own format.
- Adobe Illustrator: opens and exports SVG.
- Microsoft Edge and other browsers: show the drawing when you open the file.

**Mac**

- Inkscape and Illustrator: the same editing as on Windows.
- Safari, Chrome and Firefox: display SVG files you drag in.

**Linux**

- Inkscape: the usual choice for editing.
- rsvg-convert: the librsvg command-line tool, which renders SVG to PNG.
- GIMP: opens an SVG as a pixel image at a size you pick.

**Web**

- Every major browser displays SVG, and Figma imports it.

**Mobile**

- Phone browsers show SVG files and web pages that use them.

**Any system**

- A text editor shows the SVG's XML, which you can edit by hand.

### SVG and PNG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .svg or .svgz with image/svg+xml; .png with image/png.
- **How the picture is stored**: SVG keeps shapes and text as instructions. PNG keeps a fixed grid of pixels, compressed losslessly with DEFLATE.
- **Scaling**: an SVG redraws cleanly at any size. A PNG blurs or turns blocky when enlarged past its pixels.
- **File size**: a simple icon is tiny as SVG. A complex illustration can be larger as SVG than as PNG, and a PNG grows with its pixel count.
- **Transparency**: both have it. An SVG is clear wherever nothing is drawn; a PNG stores an alpha value for every pixel.
- **Text**: in an SVG it stays real text. In a PNG it becomes pixels.
- **Motion**: SVG can animate. This page writes a single still PNG.
- **Color depth**: PNG allows 1 to 16 bits per sample; the PNG written here has 8 bits per channel.

How this page draws it: your browser renders the SVG at the size it reports, one SVG unit to one pixel, onto a transparent canvas, and the canvas is saved as a PNG. There is no scale setting.

### Other ways to convert SVG to PNG

- **Inkscape (Windows, Mac, Linux)**: open the SVG and choose File > Export (Shift+Ctrl+E). On the Single File tab, pick Document, Page, Selection or Custom as the area, set the image size or DPI, choose PNG from the format menu and click Export. The dialog's Background Color option sets what fills transparent areas.
- **Adobe Illustrator (Windows, Mac)**: choose File > Export > Export As, pick PNG and click Export, then set the resolution and background color, which can be transparent, white or black.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux)**: open the SVG, which GIMP turns into pixels, choose File > Export As, give the file a .png name and click Export.
- **ImageMagick (command line)**: run `magick input.svg output.png`. ImageMagick draws SVG with Inkscape, RSVG or its own MSVG renderer, so results vary between them.

### Problems with SVG files

- **The PNG is smaller than you wanted**: the size comes from the width and height in the SVG. Set larger values, keeping the viewBox, and convert again.
- **Text shows in the wrong font**: an SVG that names a font your device doesn't have is drawn with a substitute. Convert the text to outlines in Inkscape (Path > Object to Path) or Illustrator first.
- **A site won't accept your SVG**: upload the PNG instead, since many forms take only raster images.
- **"Image decode failed."**: the XML is broken or the svg tag lacks its xmlns attribute. Fix the file in a text editor or re-export it from your design tool.
- **You need a JPG or an icon**: use the [SVG to JPG converter](/svg-to-jpg/) or the [SVG to ICO converter](/svg-to-ico/).

guide.title: Understanding SVG to SVG
guide.markdown:
### What is an SVG file?

Short for Scalable Vector Graphics, SVG is a W3C standard vector format written in XML. Shapes, paths and text are described mathematically, so images scale to any size without losing sharpness. It is used for logos and icons on the web, illustrations and diagrams, and charts and maps. An SVG can also embed pictures, and those parts keep their own pixel resolution when the drawing is enlarged.

SVG to SVG sounds like a no-op, but the output is a different kind of file: a picture wrapped in SVG markup.

### Programs that open SVG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Inkscape works on SVG natively, while Mozilla Firefox renders it.
- **Web and mobile:** Google Chrome displays SVG on both, and Safari does so on mobile.

### SVG and SVG compared

- **Structure**: your original holds shapes, paths and text. The result holds one `<image>` element with a PNG embedded as base64.
- **Size**: the picture is drawn 1:1 at the dimensions the browser gives the original.
- **Tracing**: none. The picture is not turned back into vector shapes.
- **Transparency**: the canvas starts transparent, so see-through areas survive in the PNG.
- **Metadata**: nothing but raw pixels passes through, so EXIF, ICC and XMP data is gone.
- **Privacy**: the drawing never leaves your device, since the page works in the browser.

### Other ways to convert SVG to SVG

These work on the SVG itself instead of replacing it with a picture.

- **Inkscape:** when you save, choose the Plain SVG type. Its manual describes it as meant for sharing your drawing with people who might not use Inkscape. Work on a separate copy.
- **Scour:** run `scour -i design.svg -o cleaned.svg`. Its options are typically lossless but can be tweaked for more aggressive cleaning.
- **SVGO:** run `svgo one.svg -o one.min.svg`. It has a plugin architecture, and the plugins are set in a config file such as `svgo.config.mjs`.

### Problems with SVG files

- **Pictures in other files vanish**: an SVG drawn as an image never loads them, online or not. Embed such pictures as data.
- **Fonts change the drawing**: the text is laid out with whichever fonts exist, so a stand-in font can alter its look.
- **Embedded pictures look soft when enlarged**: they keep their own pixel resolution. Keep your original for further editing.

guide.title: About SVG files
guide.markdown:
### What is an SVG file?

SVG is short for Scalable Vector Graphics. It is an XML-based vector image format and a W3C standard, with SVG 1.0 a Recommendation in 2001 and SVG 1.1 following in 2003. A logo, chart or icon is stored as shapes, paths and text instead of a grid of pixels, which is why an SVG can be enlarged to any size without going soft. Because the format is plain XML text, you can open the file in a text editor and read its shapes, and a text file can also be searched, indexed and compressed. The drawing can be styled with CSS, and the file can include animation and scripting. SVG also supports clipping paths, masks and filter effects. Browsers open an SVG directly, and a web page can embed one too. A gzip-compressed SVG uses the .svgz extension, and the registered media type is image/svg+xml.

Not every SVG is purely vector. Photos can be placed inside one, and they stay at their own resolution however far you zoom. A drawing can also refer to resources outside the file. A font installed on the device shows up, but a linked image or web font never loads when the SVG is drawn as a picture.

### Programs that open SVG files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- Inkscape: edits SVG natively.
- Mozilla Firefox: opens SVG files in the browser.

**Web and mobile**

- Google Chrome displays SVG.
- Safari displays SVG on mobile.

### SVG and TIFF compared

- **Content**: SVG holds shapes, text and styling you can edit. TIFF holds pixels in a tag-based structure, and one file can store several images.
- **Size**: an SVG has no fixed pixel size and scales cleanly. A TIFF is fixed at the pixel dimensions it was saved with, so enlarging it later cannot bring the sharpness back.
- **Compression and color**: TIFF allows several compression schemes, deep color and CMYK separations. SVG is XML text. The extensions .tif and .tiff both name TIFF, with the media type image/tiff, and it was developed by Aldus and Microsoft as a tag-based raster wrapper that can hold different color representations.
- **History**: TIFF began in 1986 at Aldus, and its 6.0 revision dates from 1992. Adobe now controls the specification. Classic TIFF stores file offsets in 32 bits, so a file tops out near 4 GB. SVG is a W3C recommendation.
- **Typical use**: TIFF turns up in scanning, archiving, photography and print work, and document imaging, while SVG is the logo, icon and diagram format of web pages.

The steps are short. Your browser renders the SVG and reports its width and height, and those numbers become the TIFF's pixel dimensions. The page adds no scaling, no size cap and no viewBox logic of its own, and it paints no background, so clear areas remain clear. ImageMagick, running as WebAssembly, then saves the pixels as an uncompressed TIFF whose channels are 8-bit red, green, blue and alpha. Because only raw pixels travel, EXIF data, color profiles and XMP packets stay behind. If you need more pixels, enlarge the width and height attributes in the SVG first. Your original SVG is not changed.

### Other ways to convert SVG to TIFF

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick -density 300 logo.svg logo-print.tiff`. The -density option sets the resolution ImageMagick renders an SVG at, and the default is 72 dots per inch. ImageMagick renders SVG through Inkscape, RSVG or its own internal renderer, so the result depends on the installation.
- **GIMP:** GIMP opens an SVG as an image in the usual way. Choose File > Export As to store it in a format other than XCF, and pick TIFF. The TIFF dialog offers compression such as None, LZW, Pack Bits and Deflate. GIMP opens the SVG as a picture of pixels, so keep the original SVG.

### Problems with SVG files

- **Letters are in the wrong typeface**: text is drawn with the fonts your device has, so a stand-in typeface can alter how the drawing looks. Convert the text to outlines in Inkscape before you start.
- **An image is absent**: a picture the SVG only links to is not fetched. Embed it in the file as data.
- **An embedded photo looks blurry when enlarged**: the pixel parts of an SVG keep their original resolution.

guide.title: About SVG and TTF
guide.markdown:
### What is an SVG file?

SVG is an XML format for drawings. It describes shapes, text and embedded images, and the geometry scales without losing sharpness. A font outline is only a filled shape, so strokes, text, colors and masks have no place in it.

This page turns the filled shapes of one SVG into a single glyph. Prepare the icon as one simple filled drawing; the artboard sets the height the glyph gets.

### Programs that open SVG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Inkscape edits SVG natively, and FontForge opens the finished TrueType outlines.
- **Web:** Chrome and Firefox display SVG.
- **Mobile:** Safari displays SVG.
- **Windows:** Windows Font Previewer shows a font before you install it.
- **Mac:** Font Book installs and validates font files.
- **Linux:** GNOME Fonts previews installed typefaces.

### SVG and TTF compared

- **What they hold**: an SVG holds drawing instructions. A TTF holds scalable character outlines in tagged tables, with glyph mappings, metrics and naming.
- **Origin**: Apple developed TrueType and licensed it to Microsoft. The media type is font/ttf.
- **Scale**: the font here is built at 1,000 units to the em, with the artboard (the viewBox, else width and height, else the drawing's bounds) at full height and 150 units below the baseline.
- **Limits**: a glyph can have at most 65,535 points, and a drawing past that is refused as too detailed.

The icon lands on U+E000 in a font named after your file.

### Other ways to convert SVG to TTF

- **FontForge interface (Windows, Mac, Linux):** double-click a glyph slot, choose File > Import, change the format to SVG and pick the file. Drag the outline down to the baseline, scale it with Element > Transform, then use the Generate dialog and pick the True Type outline type.
- **FontForge scripting:** `glyph.importOutlines` accepts svg files into the foreground layer, and `font.generate` takes its output type from the extension of the file name you give it.
- **IcoMoon (web):** add SVGs in the Import panel, then open the Export panel, keep the Font format ticked and download the package. Code points are set in the Metadata tab of the Batch panel.

### Problems with SVG files

- **Thin lines disappear**: a stroke becomes nothing. Convert strokes to filled outlines first.
- **Holes fill in**: a very complex shape can run past the page's time or room, and its crossing outlines then fill. Simplify the artwork.
- **Typing a letter shows nothing**: the icon is on U+E000, not on a familiar key. Type that code point to see it.
- **The font won't display**: a damaged font can fail to show; Font Book on a Mac validates font files.

guide.title: About SWF files
guide.markdown:
### What is an SWF file?

SWF is the file format of Flash, the web animation and games technology that began at Macromedia and passed to Adobe when it bought Macromedia in 2005. The letters are commonly read as Shockwave Flash, and a source also gives the name Small Web Format. One file can combine vector graphics, timeline animation, bitmap video, sound and ActionScript code. Its registered media types include application/vnd.adobe.flash.movie.

Adobe ended support for Flash Player on 31 December 2020, so SWF files now live in archives of old games, cartoons and banner ads, and it is no longer simple to see them play. An SWF may also refer to outside media instead of containing everything, so an old file can be missing parts it once loaded.

### Programs that open SWF files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- Ruffle: a Flash emulator, where compatibility depends on the ActionScript features a file uses.

**Windows and Linux**

- Lightspark: an incomplete Flash implementation.

**Mac**

- Adobe Audition: its SWF import pulls out the audio of video files, and it is not an interactive Flash runtime.

**Web**

- Web player from the Ruffle project: runs Flash in a page through WebAssembly, with some APIs still missing.

### SWF and GIF compared

- **Names and media types**: .swf is application/vnd.adobe.flash.movie. .gif is the Graphics Interchange Format that CompuServe introduced in 1987.
- **Content**: an SWF holds vector graphics, animation, video, sound and code. A GIF holds raster frames and nothing else.
- **Color**: a GIF frame draws from a palette of at most 256 colors. A SWF's vector fills and video are not limited that way.
- **Transparency**: GIF has 1-bit transparency, where a pixel is either clear or solid.
- **Sound and interactivity**: GIF has neither.
- **Compression**: GIF compresses each frame with lossless LZW.

What happens here: FFmpeg opens the SWF and builds a palette from its video frames, sampled at 15 fps and scaled to fit 480 pixels with even sides. A second pass then draws every frame with that palette and writes a GIF that repeats forever, so you do not need to choose a loop count. Only the video stream is used, so the sound is dropped and no ActionScript runs. A SWF that ran faster than 15 fps loses its in-between frames. The SWF you chose is never altered.

### Other ways to convert SWF to GIF

- **JPEXS Free Flash Decompiler:** run `ffdec -format frame:gif -export frame frames-out banner.swf`, using the executable for your platform. The wiki documents the -format option, where frame:gif is one of the frame formats. This writes each frame of the SWF as a separate GIF image in the output folder. For frame export the wiki lists PNG, APNG, GIF, AVI and SVG, with PNG as the default.
- **FFmpeg:** for a SWF with embedded video, run `ffmpeg -i clip.swf flash-preview.gif`. FFmpeg's SWF reader handles bitmap, video and audio data, and it skips vector shape tags, so it is not a Flash renderer. The reader covers FLV1, screen video, JPEG and lossless bitmap pictures, with PCM, ADPCM, MP3 and Nellymoser sound.
- **Ruffle plus OBS Studio and FFmpeg:** open the SWF in Ruffle. In OBS add a window or display capture source, click Start Recording and perform the sequence. Check the recording settings under Settings > Output first. Then encode the saved recording as a GIF with FFmpeg. This captures one playing session, including any errors.

### Problems with SWF files

- **Nothing will open it**: Flash Player was retired at the end of 2020. Use Ruffle or Lightspark instead. Lightspark is an incomplete Flash implementation, so it may not cover everything a file uses.
- **A game or animation looks wrong in Ruffle**: Ruffle has not implemented every Flash API, so graphics or behavior can differ from the original. Its compatibility page says most ActionScript 1 and 2 content will work, with some graphical inaccuracies, and that most ActionScript 3 games run well enough to be played.
- **Parts are missing**: a SWF can depend on external files that no longer exist online. Get the whole set of files.
- **FFmpeg reports an error**: the SWF probably holds no video stream, only sound or vector drawing. Try JPEXS for frames or record it with Ruffle.
- **The buttons don't work**: a GIF has no code, so ActionScript controls cannot carry over.

guide.title: About TIFF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a TIFF file?

The name TIFF stands for Tagged Image File Format, a raster wrapper first built by Aldus with Microsoft. The 6.0 revision appeared in 1992, and today the specification is under Adobe's control. Because a TIFF can use several compression methods and color representations, it serves scanners, print shops and photo archives, as well as document imaging and high-bit-depth preservation masters.

One TIFF file may hold a run of images, such as the pages of a scanned document. ImageMagick's format list describes extensive strip, tile, byte-order and compression tag controls for it. The endings .tif and .tiff both refer to the format, labeled image/tiff.

### Programs that open TIFF files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- GIMP: opens image files for editing, and each export format keeps a different part of a project's properties.
- ImageMagick: reads TIFF and writes it, with compression, strip, tile and byte-order options.

**Mac**

- Preview: lists TIFF in the format menu under File > Export.

### TIFF and SVG compared

- **What they hold**: TIFF stores pixels. SVG describes shapes, paths and text, and can also embed a pixel image.
- **Scaling**: a TIFF is fixed at its pixel size. An SVG made of paths scales cleanly, but an SVG that only wraps a picture does not.
- **Pages**: one TIFF can carry many images. The SVG produced here carries one picture, held as pixels inside an image element.
- **Color**: TIFF supports high bit depth and CMYK. SVG is XML text styled with CSS, so you can open it in a text editor, and every major browser displays it.
- **Typical use**: TIFF belongs to scanning, print and archiving. SVG is the usual choice for site logos, icons, diagrams and maps.

Here is what happens to your file. ImageMagick, compiled to WebAssembly, reads the TIFF in your browser. SVG is not a format it writes, so it produces a PNG of the picture, and the converter then places that PNG inside an SVG as one image element at the same pixel size, with a matching viewBox. The PNG data is stored in the file as base64 text. This is not tracing: no outlines are found and no text is recognized. A multipage TIFF contributes one image only, and the rest of its pages are left out. Pictures beyond roughly 537 megapixels do not convert, and the page tells you the file is too big. The result fits a tool or web page that accepts only SVG files, and your original TIFF is left unchanged. Several TIFFs chosen at once go through one after another, and each SVG is saved under the TIFF's name. For paths you can edit, trace the picture instead.

### Other ways to convert TIFF to SVG

- **GIMP plus Inkscape:** in GIMP, choose File > Export As (Shift+Ctrl+E) to store the TIFF in a format other than XCF, and use PNG. The GIMP manual points to its Files section for details on each format. In Inkscape, import the PNG with File > Import, select it with the Selector tool and open Path > Trace Bitmap. Adjust the options, update the preview and apply the trace. The vector result sits exactly above your picture, so the original stays underneath until you move or delete it.
- **ImageMagick plus Potrace:** run `magick scan.tiff scan.bmp`, then `potrace -s scan.bmp -o scan-outline.svg`. Potrace reads PBM, PGM, PPM and BMP, converts other pixel values to black and white with a threshold, and -s selects the SVG output. Unless you give a resolution with -r, it assumes the input is 72 dpi, and -o names the file the output goes to. Multiple input files are only allowed for multi-page output backends, so trace one bitmap at a time. It does not list TIFF as input, and it traces black and white shapes, so this suits a clean symbol or line drawing better than a photograph.

### Problems with TIFF files

- **A viewer shows only the first page**: a TIFF may hold several images, so use software that shows the full sequence.
- **A program rejects the file**: not every reader understands each private tag, color-profile extensions among them.
- **The file is enormous**: the original TIFF layout counts offsets in 32 bits, so files top out near 4 GB, and BigTIFF widens those fields.
